title: Trump starts building wall in Big Bend, Texas, despite landowner, business and rancher opposition
description:
Customs and Border Protection said in a statement to The Associated Press that “border wall panel installation is underway” in a 47-mile stretch of Hudspeth County in west Texas known as Big Bend 1.
There are a total of five project areas that make up the roughly 500-mile Big Bend region stretching from an area of Hudspeth County south of El Paso to Lake Amistad.
Activists said Friday they would continue opposing the border infrastructure projects in the rest of the Big Bend region, even as the panels were being installed.
In Texas, much of the opposition has centered on the agency’s plans for Big Bend National Park, in the state’s southwest on the Rio Grande that is a draw for tourists from around the world.
Earlier this week, landowners, ranchers and business owners in the Big Bend region along with a nonprofit organization dedicated to protecting the region’s landscape and heritage sued to stop the administration’s plans.
text:
The start of construction marks an important milestone in the administration’s $46 billion plan to line the border with walls, barriers, roads and technology as it seeks to make good on a key campaign promise by President Donald Trump to finish the wall. And it comes as Customs and Border Protection says it has doubled the pace at which it is building the wall across the U.S.-Mexico border.

Customs and Border Protection said in a statement to The Associated Press that “border wall panel installation is underway” in a 47-mile stretch of Hudspeth County in west Texas known as Big Bend 1. There are a total of five project areas that make up the roughly 500-mile Big Bend region stretching from an area of Hudspeth County south of El Paso to Lake Amistad.

CBP said the first panels were erected on September 15. On a map on the agency’s website where the agency posts updates of wall construction across the entire southern border, a photo showed a crane lifting one of the 30-foot-tall steel wall panels into place while construction workers looked on.

The new activity was separate from a border infrastructure project in the nearby Big Bend National Park, where the administration has temporarily suspended construction in an attempt to reach out to opponents.

Activist plan to keep up their fight

In the broader Big Bend region of Texas, CBP has run up against concerted opposition from landowners, environmental groups, business owners and ranchers who say the remote region isn’t a high-traffic area for illegal immigration.

Activists said Friday they would continue opposing the border infrastructure projects in the rest of the Big Bend region, even as the panels were being installed.

Clara Benson, one of the founders of the No Big Bend Wall Coalition which has been fighting against CBP’s plans, said in an interview Friday that the organization had been receiving reports of trucks moving supplies into the remote area along the Rio Grande and that contractors had been clearing yards to stage supplies.

But speaking from Washington, D.C. where she and others in the coalition were meeting with lawmakers, she said that the organization and others would continue to fight the wall-building plans across the region.

“We will continue to fight for this land no matter what the outcome is. We will continue fighting to the end,” said Benson. “You talk to people in west Texas and they say even if they put it up, we’ll fight for them to take it down. So this fight is not over.”

Trump has vowed to complete the border wall

The news comes as the administration is speeding forward with a plan to line the entire border with a combination of 30-foot-tall steel bollard walls, barriers designed to stop vehicles from crossing the border, new patrol roads, and various technologies to deter and detect migrants or smugglers from crossing the border.

Customs and Border Protection said it is building an average of 12 miles of barriers per week along the 2,000-mile border with Mexico and recently reached a milestone of 200 miles of new barriers built since the second Trump administration took office.

The 12-miles-a-week average is double the pace that the agency’s head, Rodney Scott, cited earlier this year.

The agency has faced opposition from environmental groups, a small town that worries the wall will cause flooding in its area, Native Americans who say the construction is disturbing sacred sites and landowners who say the construction will infringe on their land.

In Texas, much of the opposition has centered on the agency’s plans for Big Bend National Park, in the state’s southwest on the Rio Grande that is a draw for tourists from around the world. But up and downriver outside the park, much of the land is owned by private landowners, many of whom have pushed back against the government’s efforts.

Earlier this week, landowners, ranchers and business owners in the Big Bend region along with a nonprofit organization dedicated to protecting the region’s landscape and heritage sued to stop the administration’s plans.

Activists and landowners have also shown up at county meetings to push their elected officials not to cooperate with contractors hired by CBP to build the wall, and many landowners have refused to allow government officials or contractors onto their land to survey it.

title: Exiled Nicaraguan journalist detained by ICE in Florida. He could be deported
description:

His wife, Deykel Santamaría, told El Nuevo Herald, that her husband applied for political asylum in 2019 and that the case remains pending.

text:
Press-freedom groups and South Florida members of Congress are calling on federal immigration authorities to release exiled Nicaraguan journalist Luis Manuel Chavarría-Galeano after he was detained Monday by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Florida.

His detention is sparking fears that his life would be put in danger if he is deported to Nicaragua under the authoritarian regime of Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega and his wife and co-President Rosario Murillo.

Chavarría-Galeano, 48, was arrested on the morning of Sept. 14 while working as an Uber/Lyft driver in Orlando. He was then transferred to the Baker Correctional Facility in north Florida and later sent to the Krome North Service Processing Center in west Miami-Dade County.

He remains in custody at Krome pending an Oct. 2 immigration hearing, WLRN confirmed late Friday.

His wife, Deykel Santamaría, told El Nuevo Herald, that her husband applied for political asylum in 2019 and that the case remains pending.

“My husband has a very substantial asylum application file and a book of testimonies from a journalist who has been very outspoken against all the policies of the Ortega-Murillo regime,” Santamaría told the Spanish-language newspaper in Miami.

In a statement to El Pais newspaper in Spain, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said ICE agents arrested Chavarría-Galeano “during routine immigration enforcement operations” because he was “unlawfully present in the United States.”

The DHS spokesperson said Chavarría-Galeano entered the U.S. legally on December 21, 2018, and overstayed his visa, which ended on June 20, 2019.

“In violation of our nation’s laws, he remained in the country beyond the authorized period,” the DHS spokesman said. “He will remain in ICE custody while his removal proceedings are processed.”

It’s unclear if Chavarría-Galeano would be deported to Nicaragua or Spain. He also holds Spanish citizenship.

“I am strengthened in faith,” Chavarría-Galeano told Telemundo 31, a Spanish-language station in Orlando late Friday in a brief phone interview.

Speaking in Spanish, he also said he would not wish what he is experiencing at the ICE detention center on anyone.

Press-freedom advocates sound the alarm

Press-freedom organizations have urged federal immigration authorities to immediately release Chavarría-Galeano and review his pending asylum application, saying he would face persecution if returned to Nicaragua.

“This detention fits into a troubling pattern in which the Trump administration has wielded immigration enforcement against members of the press,” said José Zamora, Américas regional director for the Committee to Protect Journalists.

“It is critical that journalists who have sought asylum in the United States after fleeing persecution for their journalistic work are protected, not treated as targets for immigration enforcement,” Zamora said in a statement.

Reporters Without Borders (RSF) raised questions about Chavarría-Galeano’s detention, warning that deporting a targeted journalist back to a hostile regime creates a dangerous precedent for political exiles seeking asylum.

In a statement, Edith Rodríguez Cachera, RSF Spain’s vice president, said Spanish government officials “must use every diplomatic and consular instrument at its disposal to safeguard his security and prevent his return to a country where he will likely be targeted due to his journalistic work.”

She said the Spanish government granted citizenship to Chavarría-Galeano in July 2025.

In a joint statement released Friday, the Miami-based Inter American Press Association, along with 14 other press-freedom organizations, demanded Chavarría-Galeano’s immediate release.. They also pushed for an asylum hearing.

“The U.S. government’s targeting and detention of [Chavarría-Galeano] are a troubling escalation of attacks on journalists and media workers, particularly immigrant journalists, who consistently provide much-needed journalism and civic information for their communities,” the 15 press groups wrote in their statement.

Santamaría, Chavarría-Galeano’s wife, told El Pais: “I fear for his safety, his freedom and his integrity if he were to be sent to Nicaragua. ... He could be sent back into the hands of the same regime he fled to protect his life and his freedom.”

South Florida lawmakers: He is a political exile — not a criminal

U.S. Rep. María Elvira Salazar, R-Miami, urged the Trump administration to “enforce the [immigration] law and deport dangerous individuals, but do not treat political exiles like criminals.”

“Luis is a respected journalist who paid a price for telling the truth about the Ortega-Murillo dictatorship,” she wrote on X. “The regime persecuted him, forced him into exile, and stripped him of his citizenship.”

“That history matters,” she said. “He cannot be sent back into the hands of the people who targeted him.”

U.S. Rep. Mario Díaz-Balart, R-Miami, posted on X that he was “deeply troubled” by the detention of Chavarría-Galeano, saying the U.S. “must never lose sight of the difference between criminals and people fleeing political repression.”

Persecuted in Nicaragua for being a journalist

Chavarría-Galeano began work as a journalist in Nicaragua in the late 1990s. In 2012, he established Café con Voz, a prominent political commentary and news program that aired on the independent TV channel 100% Noticias, according to media reports.

In December 2018, following widespread anti-government protests, the Ortega regime launched a sweeping crackdown on independent media. Police raided the offices of 100% Noticias, arresting channel owner Miguel Mora and press director Lucía Pineda.

Chavarría-Galeano narrowly escaped arrest — he was out of the country on vacation at the time. He sought political asylum upon arriving in the United States on December 21, 2018, filing his formal asylum petition in 2019, according to press-freedom groups and Chavarría-Galeano’s wife.

While living in exile, Galeano continued to produce Café con Voz on YouTube and report on human-rights abuses in Nicaragua.

In 2023, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists, Chavarría-Galeano was among 94 Nicaraguans stripped of their citizenship by the Ortega government, which accused them of being “traitors to the homeland” and ordered the confiscation of their assets.

CPJ staffers said they have documented Nicaragua’s press-freedom crisis, saying 268 Nicaraguan journalists were kicked out of the country into exile, with many living in neighboring Costa Rica.

Under the Ortega-Murillo regime, the government has carried out a sweeping crackdown on dissent following a violent suppression of protests in 2018. Authorities have jailed opposition politicians, religious leaders and others, and also shut down thousands of civil-society organizations.

The congress has repeatedly amended the constitution to concentrate power in Ortega’s hands and eliminate any shred of democratic independence and dissent.

This report was supplemented with information from The Associated Press and produced by Miami Herald news partner WLRN Public Media.

text:
How far will New York Gov. Kathy Hochul go to keep immigrant criminals in this country?

So far, she’ll even pardon a man convicted of an aggravated felony, if that’s what it takes to prevent the United States Supreme Court from setting a restrictionist precedent.

Keisy Guerrero Mariano is a Dominican who spent two years in prison for committing a violent crime: second-degree assault.

Mariano, known as “G.M.” in court documents, is exactly the sort of lawbreaker Americans overwhelmingly want to see deported.

But not Hochul—she granted him clemency on Aug. 28.

His case stood out from those of the other five people she pardoned that day:

The others were nonviolent offenders who’d committed their crimes decades ago: two in the 1980s, two in the ’90s, and just one as recently as 2007.

G.M. was convicted in 2015.

The governor decided he merited special leniency for political reasons.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested G.M. in 2020, intending to deport him based on his criminal record.

ICE had to let him go in 2022, however, because of a nationwide injunction related to COVID-19 that required the agency to review the custody of individuals with certain medical conditions.

While ICE had him, though, G.M.’s lawyers challenged the agency’s right to hold him for a prolonged time without a bond hearing.

That’s what Hochul’s pardon is really about—the Trump administration planned to make the Dominican’s appeals a test case before the Supreme Court, one likely to establish that G.M. and others like him are not entitled to a bond hearing.

Bond hearings are an easily exploited weakness in America’s immigration security, not only protracting the legal process of deporting lawbreakers but also giving them an opportunity to get out of detention temporarily—and then permanently fail to show up when they’re due for their next hearing.

G.M. came to this country legally in 2011, but he forfeited any right to remain here once he committed a felony.

Only now Hochul has nullified his conviction to undercut ICE’s grounds for removing him and collapse the appeals process that was leading to the Supreme Court—and to a probable defeat for those who want to make deportation as difficult as possible.

The governor isn’t looking out for New Yorkers here:

Her maneuver is about liberal politicians’ zeal for maximum immigration, even when it means letting violent criminals remain in our communities.

This is the second lucky break Hochul’s side has had recently.

The other test case the Trump administration had teed up, involving a Jamaican national convicted (also in New York) of sexually abusing a child under the age of 11, has been taken out of the courts as well, after the offender left the country and filed a court declaration saying he would not be coming back to America.

Self-deportation is one way to get immigrants convicted of heinous crimes out of here.

But ICE can’t deport someone who has already deported himself, so his claim of a right to a bond hearing is now completely moot.

The big question still has to be answered, though: Can immigration enforcement detain these violent perps and sex offenders until they can be tossed out?

Or if they’ve been in custody for a while, are they entitled to bond hearings that will further delay their removal—and give them the chance to escape back into Americans’ neighborhoods?

Solicitor General John Sauer says he’s not going to let Hochul’s gambit succeed.

G.M.’s case may have been pulled, but Sauer aims to find another that will bring the fight to the Supreme Court.

“Mandatory deportation” should mean just that—even a legal immigrant who commits a serious offense ought to be expelled promptly, and he shouldn’t get the benefit of a bond hearing just because his case takes longer than it should and he winds up in “prolonged” detention.

He shouldn’t get the benefit of a liberal governor’s partisan machinations, either.

New Yorkers—American citizens—elected Hochul, and she should put them first, not foreigners who commit crimes while they’re here, legally or otherwise.

text:
A coalition of civil rights groups and union organizations Friday sued the Trump administration to prevent the deployment of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to polling locations during November’s midterm elections.

Earlier this summer, the Trump administration briefly indicated it would not pursue mass ICE enforcement at polling locations before officials reversed course and sparked the wave of lawsuits.

The suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia is the second this month, following comments from top Trump officials citing a federal policy to allow ICE officers to enter polling locations in certain circumstances to conduct immigration enforcement.

The groups argue the policy violates the federal law that prohibits “armed men” at election sites, and also causes voter intimidation, which is barred under the Voting Rights Act.

Under federal law, “troops” or “armed men” are allowed at polling locations only if “such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.” And the section of the Voting Rights Act the groups cite prohibits “intimidation,” “threats,” or “coercion” against a person for voting or attempting to vote.

“The result is predictable: voters across the country—particularly Black, Latino, and Asian voters, naturalized citizens, and members of mixed-status families—are afraid to vote, help others vote, and participate in civic life,” according to the suit.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin earlier this month noted that agents could conduct immigration enforcement at polling places. And before U.S. senators this week, FBI Director Kash Patel did not rule out sending FBI agents to polling locations, but said officers would “follow the law.”

The Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice did not immediately respond to States Newsroom’s requests for comment Friday.

“We reject this administration’s attempt to desecrate our polling sites by converting them into militarized zones through the unlawful deployment of ICE or any other federal agent,” Kristen Clarke, the NAACP’s general counsel, said in a statement.

NAACP is one of nine groups that filed suit. The rest are Mi Familia en Accion, Asian Pacific American Advocates, the National Urban League, Minnesota 8, the Service Employees International Union, the American Federation of Teachers, the International Union of Painters and the United Food and Commercial Workers International.

“Turning the fundamental right of exercising our vote into a high-stakes encounter with the militarized strong arm of the current administration isn’t protection and it isn’t oversight; it’s disenfranchisement, period,” Clarke said. “The NAACP calls on the court to reject this blatant attempt by federal officials to obstruct our elections through tactics pulled straight from the Jim Crow playbook.”

ICE said its pursuit of electrified shock gloves is meant to be a less violent option for officers and agents seeking to gain control of unruly individuals, reducing the need to use a Taser, baton or pepper spray.

David Venturella, acting head of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said they have not yet deployed the gloves in the field and are still in the procurement phase.

He said unlike a Taser, which shoots probes at a person, the Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, or GLOVE system, would have agents make direct physical contact with a target’s bare skin. It would send “low-level electrical pulses” that would help officers gain compliance.

Mr. Venturella, in a letter to Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, described it as “a lower level of force than other intermediate methods.”

“This technology is intended to provide officers with an additional, controlled option to de-escalate volatile situations,” the ICE chief wrote.

The system made headlines when it was first reported.

ICE critics worried about giving another tool to an agency under fire for its treatment of protesters of President Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

Mr. Grassley, Iowa Republican, had asked ICE to explain its thinking.

ICE said a pair of gloves would cost $2,495.

When an agent or officer uses the gloves, it would have to be reported as a use-of-force incident. Personnel would get annual training, on top of their quarterly use-of-force training.

The procurement documents for the gloves said they would be available to both Homeland Security Investigations, the agency’s criminal division, and Enforcement and Removal Operations, the deportation force that carries out civil immigration enforcement.

title: Appeals Court Blocks Trump Policy to Rapidly Deport Migrants to Third Countries | Truthout
authors: britney, Ariana Figueroa, Mike Ludwig, Marianne Dhenin, Sharon Zhang, Megan Rose, Andy Mannix, Ibrahim Hirsi, Sonali Kolhatkar, Victoria Valenzuela
description:
Third-country removals, deportations from the United States to a nation other than an immigrant’s home country, occur when the immigrant’s home country does not accept the person’s repatriation.
Once rare, the procedure has spiked under the second Trump administration that has entered into partnerships with several countries, some with human rights concerns, to take third-country removals from the U.S.
The Trump administration in May 2025 made an emergency request to the Supreme Court after U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy blocked the policy.
The Supreme Court in June 2025 temporarily allowed for the removals, before sending it back to the lower court.
The Trump administration later appealed to the First Circuit, and could appeal again to the Supreme Court.
text:
A federal appeals court Friday struck down the Trump administration’s policy to quickly send noncitizens to countries they are not from, finding that immigrants must have an opportunity to challenge their removal if they fear for their safety.

The decision largely upheld a Boston federal judge’s February ruling that found the Department of Homeland Security’s policy unlawful. But the immigration officers can still conduct third-country removals if they follow the proper procedures, such as adequate notice and an opportunity for an immigrant to raise a fear-based claim to that country of removal.

Third-country removals, deportations from the United States to a nation other than an immigrant’s home country, occur when the immigrant’s home country does not accept the person’s repatriation.

Once rare, the procedure has spiked under the second Trump administration that has entered into partnerships with several countries, some with human rights concerns, to take third-country removals from the U.S.

The three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit also raised doubts that a country that accepts a person that is not their own citizen could “credibly provide blanket assurances that all removed noncitizens will not be persecuted or tortured there unless it intends to provide them with some sort of affirmative protection against rogue agents and non-state actors.”

The panel also upheld the lower court’s finding that the notice to a third country was inadequate — about 24 hours — and that the policy was unlawful.

It gives “no notice at all of an impending third-country removal when the country to which the noncitizen is to be removed has provided credible (in the State Department’s judgment) diplomatic assurances that noncitizens removed there from the United States will not be persecuted or tortured,” the panel wrote.

The panel included circuit judges Lara E. Montecalvo, Jeffrey R. Howard and Seth R. Aframe. Former President Joe Biden nominated Montecalvo and Aframe. Former President George W. Bush nominated Howard.

The Trump administration in May 2025 made an emergency request to the Supreme Court after U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy blocked the policy. The Supreme Court in June 2025 temporarily allowed for the removals, before sending it back to the lower court.

Murphy again in February issued an order that blocked the policy and required DHS to carry out the statutory obligations of proper notice of removal to a third country and to give a noncitizen enough time to raise any concerns for their safety to their removal to a third country.

The Trump administration later appealed to the First Circuit, and could appeal again to the Supreme Court.

DHS did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment Friday.

text:
A coalition of 15 press freedom advocacy organizations on Friday demanded the release of Nicaraguan journalist Luis Galeano, who was arrested by federal immigration enforcement officials earlier this week.

The groups—which include Free Press, the Committee to Protect Journalists, the Freedom of the Press Foundation, the National Association of Hispanic Journalists, and Reporters Without Borders (RSF)—released a letter decrying Galeano's detention at the hands of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents on Monday.

The organizations expressed concern about Galeano being potentially deported back to Nicaragua, where he could face imprisonment for his past work exposing that government's human rights abuses. According to a Wednesday report in The Guardian, Galeano fled his home country eight years ago shortly after police raided the news outlet where he worked.

The groups also said Galeano's detention marked "a troubling escalation of attacks on journalists and media workers, particularly immigrant journalists, who consistently provide much-needed journalism and civic information for their communities."

Galeano was taken into custody despite entering the US legally in 2018 and having a pending asylum case. The Nicaraguan journalist also has a work permit and a Social Security number.

Nora Benavidez, senior counsel at Free Press, called Galeano's arrest "horrifying," while noting that the Nicaraguan is "the latest in a long line of journalists who came to the United States to report on issues of the day and instead face deportation."

"These cases aren’t just about cracking down on immigration," said Benavidez. "They are about cutting off community access to vital coverage and scaring reporters from holding those in power accountable. If our government can close off channels of exchange and the free flow of ideas, it is no more than a dictatorship."

Edith Rodríguez Cachera, vice president of RSF Spain, pointed out that Galeano was also a citizen of Spain, and urged the Spanish government to secure his freedom.

"Spain cannot stand by while one of its citizens, a journalist persecuted for doing his job, is detained in the United States and faces the risk of being sent back to a country he fled because of severe repression," said Rodríguez Cachera, "where his safety could be seriously endangered if he is deported. Spain must use every diplomatic and consular instrument at its disposal to safeguard his security and prevent his return to a country where he will likely be targeted due to his journalistic work."

Galeano's wife, Deykell Santamaría, said in an interview with El País published Thursday that she has been able to contact her husband during his detention, but she still fears "for his safety, his freedom, and his integrity if he were to be sent to Nicaragua."

Javier Melendez, a longtime friend of the detained journalist, was even blunter about what would happen to Galeano were he to be deported, describing it as nothing less than a "death sentence" in an interview with The Guardian.

The El País report noted that US Reps. María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) and Mario Díaz-Balart (R-Fla.) have expressed concerns about Galeano's detention, with Salazar saying that the US government should "always know how to distinguish between a criminal and a political exile."

text:
With arrests of immigrants rising sharply, the federal government is creating a statewide, privately operated transportation network to move detainees from local jails and police departments to ICE facilities all over Texas under armed guard, the San Antonio Express-News has learned.

GardaWorld Federal Services, a security company tied to the controversial Florida detention center known as Alligator Alcatraz, has landed a contract worth up to $382 million to provide “armed ground transportation and dispatch services" for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Texas, federal records show.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The system appears intended to help ICE handle a dramatically higher volume of detainees. Arrests of suspected illegal immigrants jumped this summer: In July, ICE made 41,850 arrests, 73% more than in the same month a year earlier.

Under GardaWorld's new contract, its employees will take custody of immigrants detained by local law enforcement agencies participating in the federal 287(g) program and drive them to ICE offices, processing centers and detention facilities. Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act allows ICE to delegate limited enforcement duties to local police and sheriffs. Six law enforcement agencies in Bexar County and thousands across the country participate in the program.

The GardaWorld contract, awarded Aug. 31, designates Bexar County as one of four Texas counties to receive priority service during the first 10 months of the armed transport program's "initial service period." The others are Dallas, Harris and Tarrant.

The system is supposed to be up and running in the San Antonio, Houston and Dallas-Fort Worth areas within 30 days and operational statewide within 120 days, according to federal contract records.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

'Exceptional situational awareness'

A GardaWorld online job posting for "armed transport officers" in San Antonio says the job pays $30 an hour with benefits and involves both "routine and high-security" transport "between state and local law enforcement partners, federal government offices and designated detention facilities."

Among other duties, the officers will search detainees for contraband, “apply and monitor restraints,” monitor “detainee behavior” and respond to “disturbances, emergencies, escape risks or operational concerns.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Job candidates must be 18 or older with a high school diploma or equivalent and a clean criminal record. They're also required to possess a registered semiautomatic handgun and a Level III armed security officer license, a credential issued by the Texas Department of Public Safety to applicants who complete an approved, 45-hour training course and demonstrate firearms proficiency.

The posting says the job requires “exceptional situational awareness” and “sound judgment when responding to security concerns or emergencies.”

The ICE contract does not authorize GardaWorld employees to make arrests or perform immigration enforcement duties under Section 287(g).

In addition to San Antonio, the job posting says transport officers will be stationed in Houston, Austin, Dallas-Fort Worth, Corpus Christi, Tyler, Abilene, San Angelo, Midland, Lubbock, Fort Stockton, Amarillo and Hallettsville. Available records do not indicate how many employees GardaWorld must hire under the contract or how many vehicles it must deploy.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

ICE and GardaWorld did not respond to requests for comment.

As it stands now, when local law enforcement officers detain someone they suspect of being in the country illegally, they call ICE to take the suspect into federal custody, and ICE drives the person to a processing or detention center. Under the new arrangement, GardaWorld will handle transportation.

The system will operate around the clock, will involve ICE facilities in Texas, Oklahoma and New Mexico, and will be coordinated by a dispatch center in the Nashville area, according to a federal solicitation for proposals.

'Texas remains the epicenter'

A request for information that ICE published in November to help the agency assess the feasibility of the program describes plans for a vast transport network with hubs near each of Texas' 254 county jails. Two full-time employees and a seven-seat SUV would be available at each location 24/7, 365 days a year.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Contractors would be expected “to respond to any location in Texas within 30 minutes,” the document states. A driver and armed guard would transport up to five "aliens" from a pickup location to an ICE office or other designated facility. “Expected tempo is two trips per hub, per shift and each trip being 100 miles on average," the request for information says.

Jessica M. Vaughan, director of policy studies at the Center for Immigration Studies in Washington D.C., a nonprofit, nonpartisan group that advocates reduced immigration to the U.S., said the GardaWorld contract “is a response to the increased number of arrests that are happening, not just in Texas but around the country."

A privately operated transport system will make it easier for local law enforcement in Texas to transfer people to ICE custody, she said, adding that it could become a model for other states.

“ICE cannot have a presence in every county, especially not in a place the size of Texas,” Vaughan said. "The most far‑flung counties are the ones that are strapped themselves with personnel. They certainly cannot spare someone to transport a criminal alien to ICE, and ICE cannot always spare someone to go get them. And so, to have a contractor ... is going to help enormously."

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

She recalled a similar arrangement in Ohio, where retired law-enforcement officers picked up people held by local agencies under ICE detainers and took them to an ICE office in Detroit.

Carolina Canizales, director of Texas campaigns and organizing, for the nonprofit Immigrant Legal Resource Center, had a less sanguine view of the GardaWorld contract.

“Texas remains the epicenter for immigration enforcement, waging state law and federal funds against immigrant communities," she said. "This contract expands that system by putting private companies in the middle of kidnapping and disappearing our immigrant neighbors. We should not be outsourcing this responsibility to a private company whose financial incentive is tied to expanding enforcement. Local law enforcement should not participate in or facilitate this system at the expense of our communities.”

Alligator Alcatraz

GardaWorld Federal Services, based in Arlington, Va., is a privately held company that provides security, medical, emergency response, disaster support, logistics and other services to federal, state and local agencies. Its Canadian parent, GardaWorld, was founded in 1995 and has its global headquarters in Montreal.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Pete Dordal Jr., GardaWorld Federal Services’ president, joined the company in 2016, according to his company biography, and lives in Austin.

GardaWorld Federal Services provided support services for the immigrant detention center in Ochopee, Fla., deep in the Everglades, that came to be known as Alligator Alcatraz.

An investigation of the facility by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general found that detainees were held for up to two hours at a time in small, cage-like enclosures with just 18 square feet of floor space.

Facility staff members referred to the enclosures as "calming areas" and said they were "for detainees to de-escalate and have time alone," according to the IG’s report, which was made public Sept. 11. The report said the use of such enclosures was "unprecedented" at ICE facilities and "does not align with standards for humane treatment."

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The facility was shuttered in June. GardaWorld said in a statement that “to our knowledge, the operations characterized as non-compliant” in the IG’s report “were not performed by GardaWorld Federal.”

Late last month, ICE hired GardaWorld to convert a warehouse on San Antonio’s East Side into a processing and detention facility for up to 1,500 detainees. The company was granted a $17.3 million contract to renovate the structure and provide "all necessary wraparound services for operation of the facility," federal records show.

'Surge in transfers'

GardaWorld's new contract to stand up a Texas-wide armed transport system for ICE coincides with a spike in detentions.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

A new analysis by the Deportation Data Project, a collaboration between lawyers and academics at the University of California at Berkeley and UCLA, found that ICE arrests rose sharply this summer after a short-lived decline following the deaths in January of Renée Good and Alex Pretti, two U.S. citizens who were shot dead by federal agents during protests against ICE operations in Minnesota.

“In both June and July, ICE made more arrests than in any previous month in the second Trump administration," the project said in a report published Thursday.

The federal agency recorded 37,917 arrests in June of this year, compared with 27,266 in June 2025 and 6,935 in the same month a year earlier, the researchers found. In July of this year, ICE made 41,850 arrests, up from 24,222 in July 2025 and 7,704 in July of the previous year.

The Deportation Data Project analysis also found “a surge in transfers from jails and prisons of noncitizens without any criminal convictions.” Of arrests that led to detention center bookings, 27% involved people with criminal convictions, the report said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Arrests made under 287(g) partnerships rose steadily this year and last, reaching about 6,000 in July, up from 612 in July 2025, the analysis found. The report said this might reflect increased funding for ICE and its expansion from about 21,000 agents in January 2025 to 29,000 in June of this year.

The number of local law enforcement agencies partnering with ICE under 287(g) is also on the rise. As of Sept. 15, the agency said it had signed 2,510 agreements with police departments and other agencies in 39 states and two U.S. territories.

The program authorizes varying degrees of cooperation. The Bexar County Sheriff’s Office has participating personnel serve ICE administrative warrants on immigrants already in custody.

READ ALSO:'Unconstitutional tactics': Texas lawmakers urge mayors to rethink partnerships with ICE

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Other law enforcement agencies in the San Antonio area cooperate under the Task Force Model, in which officers do limited immigration enforcement in the course of routine police work, such as traffic stops. Police departments in Balcones Heights, China Grove, Hollywood Park and St. Hedwig have such arrangements. So does the Bexar County Precinct 3 constable's office. The San Antonio Police Department does not.

Last month, a group of Texas lawmakers and Bexar County commissioners, all Democrats, sent letters urging local mayors to reconsider their cities’ participation in the program, saying it enabled "unconstitutional tactics."

As of July 11, 2026, ICE was holding 65,765 immigrants in detention. Of those, more than 18,000 were in ICE facilities in Texas, the most of any state, according to data compiled by the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, a research center at Syracuse University in New York.

text:
By Nate Raymond

BOSTON, Sept 18 (Reuters) - A US federal appeals court rejected on Friday a policy adopted by the Trump administration that allows authorities to rapidly deport migrants to countries other than their own without giving them a chance to raise safety ‌concerns.

Ruling in a case that is likely headed to the Supreme Court, a three-judge panel of the Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court ‌of Appeals largely upheld a February decision by a lower-court judge that declared the Department of Homeland Security's policy unlawful.

The ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by migrants subject to ​deportation orders that has become a key test of what due-process protections the government must provide before removing people to countries with which they have no connection.

"This decision confirms that due process and the protections Congress enacted against persecution and torture cannot be circumvented by putting someone on a plane to a country that was never part of their removal proceedings," Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said.

Under President Donald Trump, the administration has ‌entered into a series of agreements that have ⁠allowed it to send more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, in many cases Mexico, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.

The government is expected to appeal. Earlier ⁠in the case, the administration twice convinced the Supreme Court to lift a preliminary injunction protecting migrants' due-process rights, clearing the way for eight men to be deported to South Sudan.

The administration has also carried out third-country deportations of people to nations including Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia and the Central African Republic.

DHS General Counsel James Percival ​posted on ​X that the policy remains in force because the 1st Circuit's decision is not ​yet in effect.

"If you claim fear in your home country, ‌DHS has the right to send you elsewhere," he said.

THIRD-COUNTRY DEPORTATIONS

In March 2025, DHS adopted a policy aimed at addressing individuals who were subject to final orders of deportation but had been granted protections in immigration court against being sent back to their countries of origin.

The policy would allow migrants to be sent to alternative countries if immigration authorities have credible diplomatic assurances they will not be persecuted or tortured there.

The policy called for only minimal notice before a migrant could be sent to a third country that had not given the State Department such assurances.

US District Judge Brian Murphy, an appointee of Democratic ‌President Joe Biden, set aside the policy and concluded that it failed to protect ​migrants' due-process rights and could lead to their swift deportation to unfamiliar and potentially dangerous ​countries, without notice.

On appeal, the Trump administration contended that Murphy's order, ​if left intact, would usurp its authority to execute potentially thousands of valid orders of deportation to third countries.

But US ‌Circuit Judge Seth Aframe, writing for Friday's panel, said Murphy ​adopted a "sensible" interpretation of the immigration law ​requiring migrants be given a "meaningful" chance to raise any concerns before they are deported.

"DHS's proposed interpretation would deny access to that protection to a substantial swath of noncitizens who are sent to third countries with no notice of their destination," Aframe wrote. "We decline to adopt such ​an interpretation."

The panel included two Biden appointees, including Aframe, ‌and a judge appointed by a Republican president.

However, the 1st Circuit overturned one part of Murphy's ruling on procedural grounds. It ​concerned whether the government must first try to deport migrants to countries they have ties to before sending them to third ​countries.

(Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani and William Mallard)

text:
Federal, state, county and local elected officials, and heads of Chicago area immigrant advocacy organizations, struck a defiant note at the Sept. 9 press conference held to mark the anniversary of the Operation Midway Blitz.

During the press conference, which was held at La Villita Community Church, 2300 S. Millard St., speakers argued that the ramp up in immigration enforcement had nothing to do with detaining criminals and was meant to intimidate Chicagoans. They called upon local and county law enforcement to prosecute agents they accuse of violating residents’ civil rights. And the speakers pushed for federal immigration reform, including providing path to citizenship undocumented immigrants who came to the United States as children and immigrants with Temporary Protected Status, a program that the Trump Administration tried to discontinue.

Since shortly after the start of Donald Trump’s second term, Department of Homeland Security ramped up immigration enforcement. While 2025 saw raids that reached their apex during last fall’s Operation Midway Blitz, 2026 has seen shift in strategy, with more arrests at courthouses and worksites. The immigration courts also sought to speed up deportations, leading advocates to complain that immigrants simply didn’t have time to put on a proper legal defense.

U.S. Rep. Jesus “Chuy” Garcia, D-4th, who represents several Chicago Southwest Side neighborhoods and western suburbs that saw several high-profile incidents involving federal immigration agents, spoke first. He began his speech by paying tribute to Silverio Villegas González, an undocumented immigrant and Franklin Park resident who was killed by ICE agents during a traffic stop. A portion of Franklin Park falls within Garcia’s district. He also paid tribute to nurse Alex Pretti and Renee Good, who were killed in Minneapolis by immigration officers during Operation Metro Surge last January, as well as “all the others who have been killed by the federal government and their lawless actions.”

“But (this anniversary) is also a time of resilience, a time of resolve and the time for united resistance for the public good of all of our people,” Garcia added.

He described ICE and CBP agents as “masked, violent thugs” who “racially profiled our neighbors, pepper-strayed or neighbors and ripped children from their parents.”

“ICE’s actions were never about safety — cruelty was the point,” Garcia said.

He praised rapid response groups, volunteer organizations that sent out alerts about immigration agents’ presence and provided aid to families of immigrants who were detained. And Garcia argued that his questions during congressional oversight hearings helped pave the way from firings of Attorney General Pam Bondi and Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem.

Noting that immigration enforcement hasn’t entirely stopped, Garcia urged The Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen Burke to prosecute immigration agents for alleged excessive force and human rights violations, saying that, otherwise, it would be “sending the message that violence is acceptable if the perpetrators are employed by the DHS.” He also called for immigration reform, specifically stating Congress should create a path to citizenship for “DREAMers” — undocumented immigrants who came to the United States as children — and immigrants who were granted Temporary Protected Status, a legal status granted to refugees fleeing war, natural disasters and other dangerous conditions.

“We also need to dismantle DHS and rebuild our immigration enforcement system from the ground up,” Garcia said. “Our community and our country deserves no less.”

Unlike other members of congress who spoke on Sept. 9, Garcia isn’t running for reelection.

U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-3rd, whose district includes about a third of DuPage County, parts of the northwest and western suburbs and the northwest side of Chicago, described the past 12 months as “hell,” mentioning immigrants who were still in detention, those who have been deported, those who died, and the communities left to pick up the pieces.

“We must never normalize this,” she said. “We know there’s more to go, but we will continue to persist, we will keep us heads up.”

Ramirez also talked about the oversight role, mentioning Noem.

“I don’t want her just fired — that was good — I want her impeached and prosected,” she said. “And let’s abolish ICE, let’s dismantle DHS, and let’s create a system where we center human, justice, rule of law.”

U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley, D-5th, whose district includes parts of north and northwest Chicago, northwest Cook County suburbs and parts of western Lake County, is running to retain his seat while also collecting signatures to run for Chicago mayor. While in the past the deadline to file petitions to run for mayor was after the midterm elections, recent changes in Illinois election law shifted the deadlines to Oct. 19-26.

“I was never more proud as a Chicagoan than to see Chicago united against a common threat,” Quigley said.

He recalled an early November arrest of Diana Patricia Santillana Galeano at the North Side daycare where she worked as a teacher. At the time, Quigley and other elected officials maintained that she had a valid work permit, and Galeano was released a week later.

“My staff had to turn our office into a makeshift daycare after ICE grabbed a teacher during a morning dropoff,” Quigley said.

More recently, he said, he witnessed a deportation hearing at an immigration court where unaccompanied children were deported without a defense.

“We have work to do,” Quigley said. “We need to remind ourselves that there’s more that unites us than divides us.”

U.S. Rep. Jonathan Jackson, D-1st, whose district includes South and Southwest sides of Chicago, southwest Cook County and parts of Will and Kankakee counties, said that “President Trump tried to rip the heart out of the City of Chicago with needless aggression, confrontational behavior” and tried to turn the city “into a warzone.”

“Let’s never forget that the laws and the Constitution applies to everyone and everyone has the presumption of innocence,” he said. “And I don’t care what anyone in the Trump administration has to say — your immigration status doesn’t determine the status of your humanity.”

State Sen. Celina Villanueva, D-12th, whose district includes several West and Southwest side communities targeted in immigration raids, described Midway Blitz as a “hate-fueled campaign.”

“People who were (detained) unconstitutionally, unlawfully, U.S. citizens, legal permanent residents, undocumented people, without any, any, any thought about the Constitution of this country,” she said. “As elected officials, we’re sworn to uphold the Constitution of this country, and as state officials, we’re sworn to uphold the Constitution of this state. It’s something that I take seriously.”

The two Chicago aldermen who spoke at the conference have been affected by their operation. On Oct. 23, ICE detained two of Ald. Mike Rodriquez’s 22nd Ward staff members, including his chief of staff. They were released a few hours later.

“They were taken to a black site,” Rodriguez recalled, referring to a secret prison operated by the government. “We didn’t know where they were.”

In early October, Ald. Jessie Fuentes, 26th Ward, was handcuffed by immigration agents after asking the agents if they had a warrant to detain an injured constituent at the Humboldt Park Health hospital. The interaction was captured on video. The agents released her after taking her outside the hospital, and Fuentes has since sued DHS for damages.

“When I asked a simple question — ‘do you have a signed judicial warrant?’ — they met me with violence and handcuffs,” Fuentes said.

Rodriguez announced a day earlier that he wasn’t running for reelection, while Fuentes indicated that she was. Both aldermen said that they wanted justice for their constituents, and for their constituents to feel safe.

Several immigration advocates spoke as well. Lawrence Benitio, the executive director at Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, called for more accountability, saying that “some local stakeholders failed to meet the moment.”

“Local police agencies — do your jobs,” he said. “Investigate ICE and CBPs abuse of power, as their threat to all of us.”

text:
COMSTOCK, Texas (AP) — The Trump administration has started building the border wall through a west Texas section of the Big Bend region, marking the first major construction in an area of the U.S.-Mexico border where the administration’s plans have met heavy opposition.

The start of construction marks an important milestone in the administration’s $46 billion plan to line the border with walls, barriers, roads and technology as it seeks to make good on a key campaign promise by President Donald Trump to finish the wall. And it comes as Customs and Border Protection says it has doubled the pace at which it is building the wall across the U.S.-Mexico border.

Customs and Border Protection said in a statement to The Associated Press that “border wall panel installation is underway” in a 47-mile stretch of Hudspeth County in west Texas known as Big Bend 1. There are a total of five project areas that make up the roughly 500-mile Big Bend region stretching from an area of Hudspeth County south of El Paso to Lake Amistad.

CBP said the first panels were erected on September 15. On a map on the agency’s website where the agency posts updates of wall construction across the entire southern border, a photo showed a crane lifting one of the 30-foot-tall steel wall panels into place while construction workers looked on.

The new activity was separate from a border infrastructure project in the nearby Big Bend National Park, where the administration has temporarily suspended construction in an attempt to reach out to opponents.

Activist plan to keep up their fight

In the broader Big Bend region of Texas, CBP has run up against concerted opposition from landowners, environmental groups, business owners and ranchers who say the remote region isn’t a high-traffic area for illegal immigration.

Activists said Friday they would continue opposing the border infrastructure projects in the rest of the Big Bend region, even as the panels were being installed.

Clara Benson, one of the founders of the No Big Bend Wall Coalition which has been fighting against CBP’s plans, said in an interview Friday that the organization had been receiving reports of trucks moving supplies into the remote area along the Rio Grande and that contractors had been clearing yards to stage supplies.

But speaking from Washington, D.C. where she and others in the coalition were meeting with lawmakers, she said that the organization and others would continue to fight the wall-building plans across the region.

“We will continue to fight for this land no matter what the outcome is. We will continue fighting to the end,” said Benson. “You talk to people in west Texas and they say even if they put it up, we’ll fight for them to take it down. So this fight is not over.”

Trump has vowed to complete the border wall

The news comes as the administration is speeding forward with a plan to line the entire border with a combination of 30-foot-tall steel bollard walls, barriers designed to stop vehicles from crossing the border, new patrol roads, and various technologies to deter and detect migrants or smugglers from crossing the border.

Customs and Border Protection said it is building an average of 12 miles of barriers per week along the 2,000-mile border with Mexico and recently reached a milestone of 200 miles of new barriers built since the second Trump administration took office.

The 12-miles-a-week average is double the pace that the agency’s head, Rodney Scott, cited earlier this year.

The agency has faced opposition from environmental groups, a small town that worries the wall will cause flooding in its area, Native Americans who say the construction is disturbing sacred sites and landowners who say the construction will infringe on their land.

In Texas, much of the opposition has centered on the agency’s plans for Big Bend National Park, in the state’s southwest on the Rio Grande that is a draw for tourists from around the world. But up and downriver outside the park, much of the land is owned by private landowners, many of whom have pushed back against the government’s efforts.

Earlier this week, landowners, ranchers and business owners in the Big Bend region along with a nonprofit organization dedicated to protecting the region’s landscape and heritage sued to stop the administration’s plans.

text:
All three entities went to court this week with lawsuits designed to vacate a new Trump policy that, starting Sept. 18, denotes every person applying for a green card through a family member as a “public charge” — and therefore ineligible for a green card – if they or their minor children receive any supplemental public benefits, including SNAP, housing assistance, health insurance, benefits for workers like the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit or Pell grants for college students.

That’s a stark change from how the public charge test was determined in practice previously, which only barred people from receiving green cards if they were “primarily dependent” on government support, meaning they received cash welfare or received live-in long-term institutional care, like a nursing home, paid for through Medicaid.

Those suing argue that the rule change is illegal because it runs contrary to the Immigration and Nationality Act and over a century of policy that demands the government collectively evaluate a person’s age, health, family status, finances, education and skills when making this determination, and say it will negatively impact immigrant communities by depriving them of or chilling their access to government assistance. Receiving these types of supplemental benefits has “never” made someone a public charge in past, those suing argue.

“None of these benefits, used by citizens and non-citizens alike to build financial security and independence, relate to the type of long-term destitution recognized by Congress as making someone a public charge,” Legal Aid said in a statement. “Expanding the public charge ground of inadmissibility … has potentially life-altering adverse consequences for millions of law-abiding noncitizen residents—particularly those with low incomes and limited assets—who wish to keep their families together in the United States.”

The U.S. Department of Justice did not respond to a request for comment.

Why three green card lawsuits were filed against Trump

That each entity files its own separate suit instead of filing one large joint suit together is both intentional and important, according to attorneys representing the litigants.

They noted that is because the state, city and immigrant rights groups Legal Aid represents all experience different types of harm from the rule change, and bring different perspectives that are critical for judges to consider separately.

“All three lawsuits are very important because this rule is radical, and it attempts to penalize immigrants and their family members for using government supports that have nothing to do with their long-term prospects and their ability to achieve and maintain financial independence,” Legal Aid attorney Susan Welber told amNewYork Law. “It’s really important to get a full picture of how harmful this rule is, and the way it affects people, to have all those perspectives before the court in individual, separate lawsuits.”

Though the state, city and Legal Aid are all putting forward similar arguments on why the rule is illegal, they differ in how they communicate to the court the impacts it has on themselves and the immigrants in their care.

“The rule [is] going to have and has already started to have such a terrible effect on the organizations that we represent, which are comprised of working families, many of whom are immigrants, or serve children who are from immigrant families or who have immigrant parents,” Welber said. “The rule is going to affect their ability to help people get green cards … [and] affect their ability to provide mental health services for children, especially if those children’s parents think that they cannot keep their children in receipt of Medicaid.”

“It’s going to affect their immigration goals; it’s going to affect the amount of time and the complexity of advising clients on basic things,” she continued. “The receipt of the earned income tax credit or a Pell Grant that pays for college, or a child tax credit, is going to affect their ability to obtain a green card at some point in the future. This rule really affects our clients, these nonprofit organizations, in a very direct way that goes to the heart of what they do and what they’re trying to achieve.”

Welber says people should know that if they’ve submitted a green card application through a family member before Sept. 18 – or are applying for a green card via a different option – the rule change is likely “not legally relevant” to their immigration and public benefits options.

“The thing to understand about this new public charge rule is that it’s designed to scare people about using public benefits,” Welber said. “It really only applies to a fairly narrow group of immigrants, which is those people who are seeking to obtain a green card through a family member – there are a lot of ways to obtain a green card, but only people who obtain a green card through a family member face the public charge rule.”

The most important thing for people who are concerned to do, Welber said, is to speak with their immigration attorney or seek legal counsel through New York City’s Mayor’s Office of Immigration Affairs before making any decisions to stop receiving or to not apply for public benefits.

text:
Friday marked the start of early voting in Virginia. Voters in a handful of other states, including Idaho, Minnesota and South Dakota, can cast absentee ballots in person, typically at a local election office or voting center. More expansive early voting is scheduled to begin in those and other states in the coming weeks.

At a voting location in Fairfax, Virginia, 18-year-old college student Sanya Singhal was among the first to vote early in person Friday morning, arriving well before the site opened to get in line.

"Why not just have a little fun in life, you know, try to be the first early voter?" she said. "I really want to participate in my democracy."

At a voting location in suburban Richmond, a poll worker rang a bell as the building opened and about a dozen voters in line began to file in. Stephen Gura was excited to be the first.

"This election is critical. We need to stop the Trump agenda," said Gura, who added that he voted for U.S. Sen. Mark Warner, a Democrat, and Shannon Taylor, the Democratic nominee against Republican incumbent Rob Wittman in the 1st Congressional District.

WATCH: Trump remains focus of GOP's midterm campaign as convention wraps

The Nov. 3 election includes votes for governor and state legislature in most states and will determine whether Republicans maintain control of the U.S. House and Senate. If Democrats retake Congress, it will alter the trajectory of the final two years of Trump's term, most likely leading to investigations and other oversight efforts.

Voting underway after unusual redistricting and Trump's bid to control how elections are run

At the suburban Richmond voting center, a steady stream of voters flowed in and out. William Curry, a 74-year-old retiree who described himself as a libertarian-leaning independent conservative, voted for Warner's Republican challenger, Bert Mizusawa, and Wittman. Curry said he generally approves of the job Trump has done, apart from the war with Iran.

"He's in a mess he can't get rid of," Curry said of the conflict.

On a rainy day in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, Bill Goehring, 67, said he voted early at the county office because he will be traveling later. He voted for a mix of Democrats and independents, and said Trump's "dictatorial tendencies are bad for America."

The start of early voting comes at a time of deep angst among many Americans about issues including rising gas and grocery prices, the war in Iran, the looming risks of artificial intelligence and Trump's aggressive immigration enforcement campaign.

WATCH: News Wrap: August inflation report shows consumer prices up 3.4%

It also follows an unprecedented spate of mid-decade redistricting for the U.S. House that began when Trump urged the Republican-controlled legislature in Texas to redraw its congressional map to help the party. California and other states followed.

WATCH: Group urges Congress to adopt proportional representation to end redistricting battles

The changes affect millions of people: Research shows 1 in 10 Americans this fall is a resident of a different congressional district than in 2024.

Those partisan efforts are expected to continue before the 2028 elections after a landmark ruling this year from the U.S. Supreme Court weakened the federal Voting Rights Act's protections against racially discriminatory redistricting.

As the start of early voting approached, Trump was focused on efforts to assert federal control over election administration, even as the Constitution bestows the power to run elections on the states and, in some cases, Congress. The nation's highest court rejected Trump's bid to restrict mail ballots this week, but several of his administration's other efforts to influence the voting process and mine state voter lists for illegitimate voters continue.

WATCH: How Trump's attempt to restrict mail ballots is being challenged in court

Virginia's attorney general said Thursday that Trump's administration may have violated the state's laws after a whistleblower accused federal employees of misrepresenting themselves on voter lookup tools to hunt for noncitizen voters. In a letter, Attorney General Jay Jones demanded that the Department of Homeland Security confirm in writing whether it had directed anyone to access Virginia voters' information without first obtaining permission from those voters.

Trump for years has raised the specter of widespread noncitizen voting in U.S. elections, and this year is no exception. But research continues to show noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare.

David Becker, executive director and founder of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said he wouldn't be surprised if the Republican president continues "his disinformation campaign and his attack on election officials." But he said he thinks despite that and other challenges, "ultimately the process will hold as it has in past years."

One Friday morning voter, 63-year-old Laura Bland in Virginia's Henrico County, said she cast a ballot early to send "a signal that we're still here" amid Trump's efforts to curtail mail voting.

"Regardless of whether you vote for a Democrat, Republican, people are not going to be stopped or intimidated from participating in our elections," Bland said, nearly moved to tears as she explained her reasoning.

Advocates suggest voters cast their ballots early

Voting rights advocates have encouraged voters this year to cast mail ballots early, in part because of concerns about recent changes in U.S. Postal Service operations that could delay the application of postmarks to ballots.

"Voting early, whether in person or by mail, is good for all of our communities because it gives voters options, eases lines on Election Day and can even mean faster results," said Hannah Fried, co-founder and CEO of the voting rights group All Voting Is Local.

How Trump's attempt to restrict mail ballots is being challenged in court

"We say seven days," postmaster general David Steiner said in an interview. "Everything is solved if people vote early."

In a news briefing Thursday, Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon urged people not to be swayed by stories they might have seen or read that cast doubt on election operations. They would be able to vote "just like they always have," he said.

"I just want to reaffirm that Minnesota's elections are fundamentally free, fair, accurate, honest and secure," he said.

Swenson reported from New York and Raza from Sioux Falls, S.D. Associated Press writer Mike Catalini in Philadelphia and AP video journalist Nathan Ellgren in Fairfax, Va., contributed to this report.

title: Maga wants more babies. But they don't seem too worried about miscarriages in ICE detention
description:
While the Trump administration may want a baby boom, it won’t shock you to hear that, when you take a closer look at their particular brand of pronatalism, they don’t actually seem to want “more babies”.
A Guardian investigation published this week revealed that ICE is arresting a record number of pregnant women and teenagers.
“ICE recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration,” the Guardian writes.
It’s very strange that ICE seems to have just stopped tracking miscarriage numbers; the agency, and the Trump administration, is normally very big on surveillance.
If you suffer a miscarriage in ICE detention, possibly because of systemic medical neglect, the US government will apparently shrug and look the other way.
text:
Maga men have babies on the brain. They may not all be interested in changing diapers or hands-on parenting, but they’re very keen on population growth. “[W]e want more babies, to put it very nicely,” Donald Trump said last year.

Trump, who has called himself the “father of IVF” and joked that he will be known as the “fertilization president”, surrounds himself with people who profess a similar fondness for children. Only a few days after being sworn in as vice-president, JD Vance declared he wanted “more babies in the United States of America” and went on to make pronatalist policies a theme of his time in office.

Meanwhile, the administration’s favourite moneyman, Elon Musk, is doing his own part to increase the population. Ashley St Clair, the mother of one of his many offspring, has claimed he once told her he wanted to have “a legion of children before the civil war”. At least one of Musk’s kids has denounced him, so I’m not sure he’s considered that they might not all be fighting on the same side.

While the Trump administration may want a baby boom, it won’t shock you to hear that, when you take a closer look at their particular brand of pronatalism, they don’t actually seem to want “more babies”. What they really want, judging by the way in which pregnant immigrants are being treated, is more of the “right” type of baby.

A Guardian investigation published this week revealed that ICE is arresting a record number of pregnant women and teenagers. These detained women are reportedly not receiving the prenatal healthcare they need and, alarmingly, ICE does not seem to have records of how many of these women have suffered miscarriages.

“ICE recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration,” the Guardian writes. “[B]ut the agency has no data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025.” Let me just reiterate that: we have no idea how many women in ICE detention have lost their babies over the past 11 months.

It’s very strange that ICE seems to have just stopped tracking miscarriage numbers; the agency, and the Trump administration, is normally very big on surveillance. Last year, the Guardian reported that pregnant immigrant women were turning up to hospitals to deliver their babies wearing location-tracking smartwatches as part of an ICE monitoring program. One of these women was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia, which can cause major swelling, and hospital staff were worried that the smartwatch would cut off her circulation. “She was in tears about [the idea of taking the surveillance device off],” a hospital staffer told the Guardian. “She had this deep fear that ICE was going to come to the hospital and take her baby.”

Surveillance also extends to the broader pregnant population. When Dr Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) earlier this year, she emphasized: “Abortion surveillance is absolutely a critical component of what the CDC is currently doing.” While the CDC doesn’t require states to collect data on abortions, 44 states plus Washington DC have some sort of mandated abortion reporting, according to the Guttmacher Institute. This isn’t necessarily sinister but, following the overturning of Roe v Wade, there has been growing concern that this data might be weaponized to punish abortion patients and providers, who are increasingly being treated like criminals.

And that concern is hardly unfounded. In the first two years after Roe was overturned, prosecutors in 16 states charged more than 400 people with pregnancy-related crimes, a 2025 report by the group Pregnancy Justice found. The report also noted that there are likely far more cases of miscarriage criminalization than have made headlines.

Funny, isn’t it? If you suffer a miscarriage in ICE detention, possibly because of systemic medical neglect, the US government will apparently shrug and look the other way. But if you have a miscarriage in a state that has fetal personhood language in its abortion laws, you may find yourself facing a police investigation and criminal charges. Once again, there is nothing pro-life about this administration. They are solely pro-control.

FBI warned ICE agents could be targeted by fake ‘tradwife’ dating profiles

“These profiles were incorporating imagery of a ‘traditional wife’ aesthetic and listing specific interests in an attempt to appeal to … individuals in law enforcement,” an internal FBI memo warns. “The objective was to lure affiliated law enforcement personnel into an online or in-person interaction under the guise of a date, after which the individuals would be publicly exposed and doxed online.” Oh dear, my heart bleeds for these poor ICE agents.

Turkey is targeting LGBTQ+ activists and journalists

Starting last Sunday, Turkish police raided the offices of LGBTQ+ rights organizations and HIV-advocacy groups. Then they arrested people protesting against the raids and journalists covering the protests. “This is the widest crackdown on LGBTQ+ people in recent years,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, of Human Rights Watch. Homosexuality isn’t illegal in Turkey, but the government seems to be weaponizing “obscenity” laws to target the community.

Israeli ‘double tap’ strike kills child and medic in Gaza

The “ceasefire” continues.

Women ‘less likely to be offered active treatment’ than men with the same condition

New research from the University of St Andrews found that women have significantly unequal medical care. Men are far more likely to be offered treatments such as strong painkillers or surgery, according to the analysis.

Joe Rogan calls Trump supporters ‘nuts’ and ‘rabid’

Does the podcaster not realize that his support helped get Trump elected? Lack of self-awareness aside, it’s amusing to watch some of Trump’s former supporters turn on the president.

Michigan high school asks girls to share details of menstrual cycles

Female students who miss swimming because of their periods need to have a parent submit a note “stating the length of the menstrual duration” so they can make up the day. If you don’t comply, your grade is at risk.

Indonesia’s all-female firefighting team are battling peatland blazes and patriarchal attitudes

One hundred and forty-six women, aged between 20 and 58, make up the Power of Mama, which protects the biodiverse region of Indonesian Borneo. “Because we are housewives, we are the ones that feel its effects most,” one member said of what motivated her to fight fires. “I thought I had to do something about it.”

Kash Patel defends new FBI bestiality policy

Patel told a Senate judiciary committee oversight hearing that the FBI “did not want to punish victims of bestiality” by automatically disqualifying them. At one point of this absurd hearing, a senator from Louisiana asked Patel whether the change “disqualified the animal” from FBI service. Just when you thought US politics couldn’t get any more stupid, it goes and surprises you.
