text:
‘Pulled off the plane’ – Deportation stayed for York pastor, Haitian immigrant

Intervention from elected officials allegedly influenced decision.

Jordan Wilkie/WITF

As the democracy reporter for WITF, I will cover any kind of story that has to do with how we govern ourselves. That will include doing a lot of election coverage about how to access the ballot, how public officials administer elections, the technology used to run and secure elections, and the laws that govern it all.

My work will also include accountability coverage for elected officials that use their positions to then undermine democratic institutions, like the legislators that voted against the certification of the presidential election results on January 6, 2021. If that weren’t enough, I foresee covering some local government decisions, fights over public records and transparency, and some candidate coverage around the major elections. As seen in my coverage of immigrant of LGBTQ+ communities, I also report on the consequences of elections for minority groups.

A York pastor and father of two U.S.-citizen children was loaded on to a deportation flight to Haiti, but was removed at the last minute, according to immigration advocates.

They are celebrating the momentary win while calling for continued support for the legal challenges ahead in the case of Molis Augustave.

“Molis called his wife last night and he let her know that he was indeed loaded onto that plane yesterday morning,” said Ama Frimpong, lead attorney for the immigration rights group We Are CASA. “He was scared as he was being loaded onto that plane, as he was being marched onto that plane. He was so terrified. And he was, indeed, taken off the plane at the last minute.”

Public outcry and political intervention kept Augustave from being flown to Haiti, according to Frimpong.

“What is different about this case is the fact that people were paying attention, is that people we’re calling their elected officials. People were making noise,” she said.

She and the legal team she is coordinating filed a flurry of legal appeals to try to keep Augustave on U.S. soil, but none of them worked. Augustave, who was being held at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center, was transferred to a “staging facility” in Alexandria, Louisiana, where deportation flights to Haiti first got to Miami, then out of the country.

In an emergency hearing Thursday, federal judge David Joseph in the Western District of Louisiana denied a request for a temporary restraining order against the federal government to stop the deportation.

Augustave was instead spared deportation, for now, due to political intervention, according to We Are CASA’s national communications director Jossie Flor Sapunar.

She said that Gov. Josh Shapiro and Sen. John Fetterman, Democrats, and Sen. Dave McCormick and Congressman Lloyd Smucker, Republicans, all intervened to keep Augustave in the country.

Smucker’s office said federal privacy protections prevent the office from discussing individual cases. None of the others responded.

“It’s really all-hands-on-deck from faith leaders, from national organizations, from statewide and local organizations,” Sapunar said.

Few immigrants receive this much support. Augustave previously worked for We Are CASA and has longstanding connections to advocacy groups like the Haitian Bridge Alliance. Based in San Diego, near where Augustave crossed the border in 2016, the nonprofit supports Haitian immigrants. His case has received extensive local media attention, as well as coverage from the Miami Herald, which first covered Augustave’s deportation stay, and Christian outlets focused on his role as a pastor.

Most detained immigrants do not have lawyers, and the vast majority of those without representation lose their cases.

The Department of Homeland Security, in a statement issued by an unnamed spokesperson, did not confirm details of Augustave’s story. The agency does not discuss details of removal flights for security reasons, the spokesperson said.

The next legal battle

Frimpong and Augustave’s legal team made another flurry of legal filings once his deportation was stayed on Thursday.

They have now made emergency motions to reopen his case and block deportation, both with the Board of Immigration Appeals. Lawyers in Louisiana are also pursuing a habeas corpus claim, used to challenge Augustave’s detention and to get them released while the case plays out.

“We have secured additional time for all of these reviews to happen, but it does not end here,” Frimpong said. “We must remain alert, we must remain vigilant, and we must make sure that we hold the Department of Homeland Security accountable to its duties.”

DHS said Augustave entered the country illegally, while his legal team said he’s done everything the right way. Neither group has provided legal documents to prove their side, and immigration cases are largely protected from public disclosure as is required in other civil or criminal cases. Sapunar said they first need permission from Augustave.

What is clear is that until July 27, Augustave and more than 15,000 other Haitians living in Pennsylvania and more than 330,000 nationally were protected from deportation because the federal government felt Haiti was too dangerous to send people back. The Trump administration tried to remove those protections in 2025, were challenged in court, and eventually won in front of the U.S. Supreme Court earlier this year.

Haiti has a collapsed government, is largely controlled by gangs, has 1.5 million internally displaced people, and the U.S. government advised no one travel there because it’s too dangerous.

A ‘draconian’ system

Augustave may need more political help to get released from detention, have his case reopened and deportation order cancelled, and to have his separate green card application with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services be accepted.

DHS’ spokesperson said Augustave “will remain in ICE custody pending removal.”

Frimpong said President Donald Trump’s second administration has turned USCIS into another immigration enforcement arm. She warned of the possibility of the green card application being dismissed as an act of retaliation for the advocacy surrounding Augustave’s request.

Trump also reshaped the Board of Immigration Appeals, which oversees two key parts of Augustave’s legal battle, by firing the 13 judges appointed during the President Joe Biden administration. He has also fired over 100 immigration judges, even as the system sees growing backlogs from aggressive immigration enforcement.

Kerry Doyle was one of those judges. Before moving into that role, she was ICE’s top lawyer and the deputy general counsel for DHS in the Biden administration.

“It’s very clear that this administration has used a very heavy hand in pushing its own agenda on both the Board of Immigration Appeals as well as the immigration courts,” Doyle said. “People are not getting their due process; they’re not getting a neutral arbiter when they go into immigration court.”

Unlike other federal judges, immigration judges are employed by the Department of Justice and are not part of a separate, independent branch of government. Doyle is now an immigration lawyer with Green & Spiegel. She is not involved in Augustave’s case.

She said the speed with which Augustave was moved from detention to attempted deportation is unusual for any administration before Trump’s second term.

West Manchester Township police in York County stopped Augustave Sept. 4 for a broken headlight, then turned him over to ICE for deportation. The flight he was supposed to be on took off Sept. 17.

It’s especially unusual for a case like Augustave’s, Doyle said.

“Why are we wasting our time and energy in traumatizing this family and this individual when he will have to get his case reopened,” she said. “If the case is reopened, he could apply for permanent resident status or green card and be a permanent resident in a month or two months and continue to be a contributing member of society. But instead, they want to throw him on a plane and traumatize him, traumatize the family, and put him in a country that is in civil war.”

Deportation flights can’t even go to the capital city, Port-Au-Prince, anymore due to the instability, Doyle said.

Augustave has no criminal history. He’s been in the country since 2016. He’s married to a U.S. citizen, and the USCIS already accepted his I-130 application, which shows the marriage is legitimate and opens the door for applications for permanent residency, though it doesn’t protect from deportation.

The Trump administration has overstepped in places, as seen by lawsuits against some of its practices, but it is largely operating within the scope of immigration enforcement powers granted by Congress, Doyle said.

On paper, the last major rewrite of immigration laws in 1996 created a system that “really is quite draconian,” Doyle said.

“We had never seen the law being taken to its fullest, and now we are,” she said.

Prior administrations prioritized different groups for arrest and deportation. On the campaign trail, Trump claimed he would focus on criminals, but Doyle said this administration’s only priority is high deportation numbers. That’s been reflected in Trump’s own goals, pushing DHS to deport 3,000 people a day — a number it has not achieved, but is still setting records for removals, largely with the help of local law enforcement like the officers that stopped Augustave.

text:
KINGSTON, Jamaica (AP) — A deal to accept migrants expelled by the United States is sparking protests by Jamaica’s main opposition party and a host of other groups.

The deal was signed on June 10 by the U.S. and Jamaica, which this week finished rules meant to defuse public anger about it. The agreement allows the Trump administration to send non-Jamaican migrants to the island en route to their home countries.

Jamaica is joining nearly 30 nations that have agreed to accept migrants expelled by the U.S. The opposition center-left People’s National Party, along with civic organizations, commentators and members of the Jamaican diaspora, is demanding that the ruling conservative Jamaica Labour Party go beyond this week’s rules and disclose the details of the agreement.

PNP officials say they worry about strains on resources and national security, and human rights protections for migrants. They have also expressed fears that Jamaica could incur unexpected costs or take in individuals with criminal histories.

“We just don’t trust what the government is saying,” said Bishop Alvin Bailey, leader of an alliance of evangelical churches.

Jamaica’s ministries of national security and foreign affairs have said the new rules stipulate that the U.S. will assume the cost of the deal and not send any migrant with a criminal record.

Jamaica also says the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration will meet migrants' needs while they are in the country.

The PNP’s national security spokesman, Fitz Jackson, said that citizens should know what their country has agreed to. The document laying out the deal also must be approved by Parliament, he said.

“Jamaicans are being asked to trust a secret document that touches their security, their communities and their public services,” Jackson said.

Foreign Affairs Minister Kamina Johnson Smith said that Washington is opposed to the details being made public. The State Department said it didn’t comment on communications with other governments.

“They have not generally released their agreements, and they have not agreed to release this one,” Johnson Smith said.

text:
Doral Mayor Christi Fraga is responding to business owners who say increased immigration-enforcement activity in the city is frightening customers and workers and taking a significant toll on their businesses.

ICE agents were seen Wednesday in different areas of Doral, a city with a large immigrant population. A social-media platform reported that agents detained people at a gas station near Northwest 41st Street and 107th Avenue.

Nearby business owners say the presence of immigration agents is having an economic impact.

“ICE agents have been very close to our area, on 107th Avenue. People are scared to come out. It’s affecting us,” said Katia Rios, of Pipo Burgers.

Rios said the business has experienced a dramatic decline in customers.

“Our sales have dropped 70%. We spend hours empty,” she said.

Fraga told CBS News Miami that she understands the concerns but said local governments have no authority to prevent federal immigration agents from conducting enforcement operations.

“I don’t agree with the way things are handled,” Fraga said.

“This is federal law. We cannot impede the federal ICE agents from coming into the cities and doing their enforcement, whether we agree or not,” she added.

Before dusk Wednesday, cellphone video captured another arrest by agents in Doral, this time in the middle of traffic.

Fraga said the city does not receive advance notice when federal immigration agents conduct operations within Doral.

“No, the city is not notified when they are in our city,” she said.

For some business owners, the impact extends beyond declining sales.

“We want to see action,” said Angelica Yepez, a restaurant co-owner who said she is down to one employee after losing six workers who feared being detained despite having applied for political asylum.

Yepez said she wants city leaders to meet with affected business owners and explain what, if anything, local officials can do.

“I want the mayor and elected officials to meet with us and tell us, ‘This is what we can do,’ ” Yepez said.

The concern is also being felt by businesses outside Doral.

Miguel Angel Flores owns a food truck near the city and said he, too, has been affected by the fear surrounding immigration enforcement. Holding back tears, Flores said, “I’d like to be out in the streets and not be scared.”

Some business owners told CBS News Miami they do not believe letters and emails from city officials are enough.

Fraga said the city’s efforts go beyond written correspondence.

“It’s not just emails and letters. There are phone calls being made,” she said. “We are doing what we can to have conversations. I know it’s a very difficult time. I recognize it.”

Doral’s demographics make immigration enforcement an especially significant issue for the community. Census data show a large majority of the city’s population is foreign-born, with Venezuelans making up a substantial portion of Doral residents.

For business owners like Rios and Yepez, the concern is not only about immigration enforcement itself, but also about what happens when customers and workers become too afraid to leave their homes.

As ICE enforcement continues in and around Doral, they are asking city leaders for more direct assistance — while the mayor says the city’s ability to intervene in federal immigration operations is limited.

text:
A federal immigration agent who shot and wounded a man in north Minneapolis this winter pleaded not guilty in federal court in St. Paul on Friday to charges of lying to the FBI.

On Friday morning, U.S. Magistrate Judge Elizabeth Cowan Wright set Christian Castro's bond at $75,000 with conditions, including that he not break any laws and only travel between Minnesota and Texas. Castro must also stay in his residence from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m. and go through a mental health evaluation.

Wright ordered the parties to submit a motion to designate the case as complex and the proposed schedule for the case by Oct. 2.

Castro, 52, is also facing state assault charges for the shooting on Jan. 14. Castro is accused of firing through the closed door of a home and injuring Julio Sosa-Celis, an immigrant from Venezuela, after a car chase involving Sosa-Celis' roommate Alfredo Aljorna.

The judge overseeing the state case set Castro's bond Thursday at $200,000 with conditions that include pre-signing a waiver of extradition, surrendering his passport and electronic home monitoring. He's also not allowed to talk with other ICE agents.

Prosecutors in the state case argued that Castro was a flight risk due to numerous phone conversations he had in prison with a Mexican resident about potentially purchasing property there. Castro posted bail and was released from the Hennepin County jail by Thursday evening.

The Department of Homeland Security initially claimed that the federal agent was assaulted by men with a broom and shovel and charged Sosa-Celis and Aljorna. That narrative fell apart and charges were dropped against the two men after footage emerged from a Minneapolis surveillance camera on the street. After being released from Texas jail, Castro was indicted by a federal grand jury on six counts of lying to the FBI.

Castro was arrested in downtown Minneapolis by state Bureau of Criminal Apprehension agents on Wednesday. His attorney said Castro had planned to surrender to state authorities. But Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said on Thursday that Castro hadn't followed directions. State Attorney General Keith Ellison said on Thursday that he was dropping a lawsuit against the state of Texas over Abbott's failure to extradite Castro.

"I hope I'll never have to file another like it because we expect and we pray for cooperation between the states, as the Constitution requires," Ellison said. "But of course, if we ever have to, we won't hesitate to use the rule of law to seek justice for Minnesotans."

Rep. Adelita Grijalva said that the "ultimate responsibility lies with" the White House, which sent the men "into harm's way."

The human rights group issued an urgent appeal, calling on supporters to send letters to the vice president of Equatorial Guinea, Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue, saying that that Ahmed Soliman, an Egyptian national, and Samson Birhane, who is from Eritrea, were "beaten and violently taken by police officers from the Hotel Bamy in Malabo," the capital of Equatorial Guinea.

They had been "arbitrarily" held at the hotel along with dozens of other people since US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) sent them there on deportation flights earlier this year. Soliman and Birhane had protection from refoulement to their countries of origin from US immigration courts, but President Donald Trump's administration has arranged with five governments, through direct payments of tens of millions of dollars in taxpayer money, to send hundreds of migrants to countries where they have never lived—many with records of human rights abuses.

Soliman has publicly spoken out against their arbitrary detention, and international media recently published a video showing a police officer at Hotel Bamy pointing a weapon at him and another man.

Last Friday, days after the video went public, said Amnesty, Soliman and Birhane were "targeted" by police, who arrived at the hotel and took them away briefly.

Amnesty continued in its letter and call to action:

Later during the day police officers went back to the hotel, bringing Ahmed Soliman and Samson Birhane back with them, who had their heads covered with bags tied with a rope. Police officers beat them in their heads, backs, and ribs with their elbows, knees, and guns, asking them where they hid the phones. They pushed one of the men down the stairs of the hotel and said to others that they may never see Ahmed Soliman and Samson Birhane again.

The group wrote that the men were taken "the Malabo gendarmery station known as 'La Luna'" and were accused of breaking a mirror at the hotel.

"Since then, they have not been informed of the charges against them, nor allowed to speak to their lawyers, and are held in an overcrowded police cell, in inhumane conditions," reads the sample letter. "I am concerned that they are at heightened risk of torture."

The New York Times reported that a lawyer who has been able to get some information about Soliman and Birhane's condition said they have been denied food and are "covered in bruises."

"The authorities must immediately release them, inform them of any charges against them, and allow them unimpeded access to counsel," said Amnesty International.

text:
Last week, Renatho Casseus was attending classes at San Diego City College like any other student. Now, he’s being held in a building surrounded by barbed-wire fences.

Just over a week after the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents arrested Casseus near San Diego City College, the student faced his first bond hearing at Otay Mesa Detention Center. Casseus was denied bail. The incident continues to reverberate through the City College community.

City College president Ricky Shabazz has been closely following the case. He was at the 8 a.m. bond hearing.

“What I saw was a young man who very simply said get me out of here so I can go back to school,” Shabazz said. “And the fact of the matter is that he’s caught between a political system and an immigration system that is broken. And we’re doing everything we can to provide support to the family at this time.”

Casseus is a Haitian immigrant who is seeking asylum in the United States, his attorney said. Shabazz said the young man supported his family by driving his parents to and from work, working part-time jobs while in school, and attending San Diego City College in hopes of continuing to build a better life.

Since his detainment, the San Diego City College community has raised more than $10,000 to support Casseus' legal fees. The judge in the case, however, ruled that they lacked the jurisdiction to release Casseus on bail.

Casseus' attorney, Wismick Saint-Jeans, said his client's continued detainment will prevent him from making substantial progress on Casseus' pending asylum case — a process that goes much smoother when working together in person

“He could come to my office where we can sit down and talk about this. We can help him craft declarations, and then have him fill out his asylum application, and tell him what evidence we need to help prove his case,” he said. “All these things need to be done, I can’t do them with Renatho being on the (inside).”

Casseus' arrest came months after the Supreme Court ended Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitian and Syrian immigrants. But removing TPS does not automatically mean Haitians seeking asylum are in the country illegally, Saint-Jeans said. Many Haitian people who applied for TPS have also applied for other immigration benefits.

“All those benefits are still in place and are preventing deportation,” he said.

The incident has caused an outpouring of both anger and support at San Diego City College. The plaza near where Casseus was taken into custody is now covered in anti-ICE messages and protest art.

Some students and faculty are urging lawmakers to consider new legislation that could help create a safer space around the inner-city campus.

“I do think we our administrators and local politicians need to help us to create this legislature so that way we feel safe coming to class consistently and people don’t feel like they have to drop out or miss class and fall behind,” said Zavahna Chavarin, who is a student and member of several social justice groups on campus.

Because San Diego City College is situated in downtown’s urban landscape, Chavarin hopes that new laws could help extend protections against immigration enforcement beyond the campus’ boundaries. That includes protecting the bordering city streets students must cross to reach many of their classes.

Students and faculty are also calling for an investigation into City College campus police who were present on the day of his arrest.

Footage from the arrest shows ICE agents speaking with a campus police officer, according to professor Mona Alsoraimi-Espiritu. It is unclear what transpired in the conversation. But witnesses of the event claim that the officer may have helped direct traffic before Casseus’s arrest, making it more difficult for him to escape.

“To anybody who sees that, what it looks like is that they made it easier for ICE to do their jobs,” Alsoraimi-Espiritu said.

The district policy prohibits public agencies from participating in immigration enforcement activity. If approached by ICE, City College employees have been instructed to ask agents to leave campus.

“That to me is the only appropriate way to respond to these situations because anything more than that is helping them,” she said.

The student group Students for Justice in Palestine (SJP) has filed formal complaints with the district regarding the campus police activity. They are asking for an investigation and for the officer involved to be placed on administrative leave.

The Academic Senate, a faculty-led governing body, also passed a recent resolution advocating for police accountability.

text:
(CN) — Four men testifying Friday to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s arrest and detention practices in Oregon said they were asked few, if any, questions before they were taken to detention facilities hours away from their homes.

Speaking through Spanish interpreters, the men — all in their 20s and 30s who work in blue-collar and service-connected jobs — said they still fear arrest by ICE and potential deportation, despite the fact that they are following immigration laws.

Their testimony bolstered arguments from a class of Oregon immigrants who want U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai to ensure the government is complying with his February injunction preventing ICE agents from arresting Oregon residents without a warrant and without determining whether they posed a flight risk.

The order provided them with new rules and parameters for how to perform an arrest that comported with the law.

A 34-year-old man from Venezuela, known only as JCCV, living in The Dalles, Oregon, with his family, said that he had a pending immigration application when he was inexplicably detained and taken to a Portland facility for multiple days.

He said agents mistook him for his brother, who is also living in the U.S., but didn’t bother to check his identification.

JCCV and other witnesses described being pressured by agents into signing a document for voluntary self-deportation.

“Before you signed it, did anyone explain to you that you were signing a document that would cause you to be removed from the country?” Kasubhai asked the man.

“No,” he said.

“What documents were the language in?”

“English.”

“Can you read English?”

“No.”

“Would you have signed the documents if they told you it was a form for voluntary departure?”

“No.”

Nelly Paola Garcia Orjuela, an attorney with the Innovation Law Lab, said the warrantless arrests were part of the Trump administration’s efforts to hit immigration arrest quotas to conform with the president’s sweeping deportation program.

“This meant a contingent of ICE agents were deployed to arrest many Oregonians without a warrant, detain them and transfer them out of state. Defendants did not discontinue this practice, and it’s because defendants continue to defy the law and are not complying with the law is why we are here today," Orjuela said.

Specifically, Orjuela accused ICE of making flight risk assessments of arrestees after their detention, applying improper flight risk standards, underreporting arrests and redacting and withholding arrest data meant to ensure compliance with the judge’s order, among other things.

Amber Qureshi, an attorney with the Deportation Data Project, which publicizes immigration enforcement data through Freedom of Information Act requests and other sources, testified there were 574 immigration arrests in Oregon between the judge’s February order and July.

Of those, 504 have been noncustodial arrests, which means they are more likely to have occurred without an arrest warrant, she explained.

At the end of an all-day evidentiary hearing, the judge signaled support for the request.

“At the minimum, the attention behind the document disclosure ordered in the preliminary injunction is not being met,” Kasubhai, a Joe Biden appointee, said. “I need to revisit what is being required to ensure the respondents are complying with my preliminary injunction.”

On cross-examination, the DOJ attorneys attempted to poke holes in witness testimony, questioning the validity and consistency of their statements.

“Plaintiffs bear the burden of demonstrating defendants have the violated injunction by clear and convincing evidence. They have not met that burden," DOJ attorney Ariana Garousi said.

Department of Justice attorneys argued that the men all had warrants for their arrest, which necessitated their detention.

Kasubhai also expressed confusion over ICE’s use of previously issued warrants to re-arrest immigrants.

“The idea that a warrant is issued and then someone is taken into custody and released generally means that the warrant is now resolved, and if somebody wanted to take that individual back into custody there would have to be an issuance of another warrant,” he said. “That doesn’t mean that the underlying issue has been resolved, but a new warrant has to be issued.”

But the DOJ attorneys argued that is not what Department of Homeland Security regulations require.

DOJ attorneys only called one witness, an ICE agent in the Medford, Oregon, known as JG who described the arrest of two of the witnesses. The hearing will continue Monday.

text:
Costa Rican content creator Julián Valverde, known online as Julián Valjota, is in the custody of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. A source close to the case confirmed his custody, and said the 26-year-old, whose full name is José Julián Valverde Meneses, is being processed by US immigration authorities.

Costa Rican journalist Elías Alvarado confirmed on Thursday night that Valverde was detained on Wednesday, in Orlando, and the reasons have not been made public. Alvarado said people close to Valverde told him that Orlando police stopped the creator while he was driving.

Alvarado also said no official information yet establishes the circumstances of the detention, Valverde’s current immigration status, or whether he faces a final order of removal from the United States. Before the custody confirmation, Alvarado had said Valverde did not appear in ICE records.

The detention became public yesterday through fellow content creator Christopher Araya, known as Araya Vlogs. In a video, Araya said Valverde had been held for nearly 24 hours and had not yet appeared before a judge. He added that the group was in contact with Valverde’s attorney and with lawyers who specialize in immigration.

Araya said Valverde had asked him to share the news in order to head off rumors. Valverde’s last social media post, published Wednesday night, was a video recorded inside his car with a patrol vehicle visible behind him. Costa Rica’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it is following the case. The ministry’s Consular Department and the Consulate General in Miami said they are aware of the situation and are making inquiries with US immigration authorities to learn more about the citizen’s circumstances.

The case also reached the Legislative Assembly. Frente Amplio lawmaker Joselyn Sáenz called on the Foreign Ministry to act to protect Valverde and all Costa Ricans held by ICE in the United States. She also criticized ICE over what she described as alleged inhumane, degrading and discriminatory treatment.

Valverde has lived in the United States for more than five years and left Costa Rica in search of work opportunities. He has frequently joked in his content about a possible deportation, though those remarks do not establish his current immigration status or explain this week’s detention.

Costa Rica is among the countries whose citizens are subject to mandatory consular notification when arrested or detained in the United States. US authorities must therefore notify the relevant Costa Rican consulate without delay.

The next steps depend on facts not yet made public. If a final removal order exists, ICE could move ahead with his departure, including arranging travel documents. If he has an open immigration case, a pending protection claim or another legal avenue to challenge removal, his attorneys could pursue those remedies.

text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent told Newsweek she was effectively forced out of a job after reporting concerns about detention conditions and the way she was treated in the workplace through official whistleblower channels.

Lenicia Shannon, a 46-year-old deportation officer assigned to ICE's Miami Field Office in Stuart, Florida, said she reported alleged discrimination, harassment, misconduct, and detention-related concerns to the U.S. Office of Special Counsel (OSC), an independent federal watchdog responsible for protecting federal whistleblowers and investigating retaliation complaints.

She accused ICE of failing to adequately investigate complaints she filed with federal oversight bodies, and said the agency subsequently retaliated by issuing a Letter of Counseling, referring her for a fitness-for-duty evaluation, suspending her law-enforcement authority, and ultimately placing her on paid administrative leave.

Read More on U.S.

ICE records provided by Shannon and reviewed by Newsweek showed that the agency later accused Shannon of disruptive and combative conduct during a February 2026 reasonable-accommodation meeting, allegations she denies. Other records reviewed show that, before those actions, Shannon received multiple commendations, leadership recognitions, and awards from the agency.

"When you report it, you become a target," Shannon told Newsweek in an interview. "You’re the victim, and they make you the adversary."

When reached for comment on the allegations, a spokesperson for ICE told Newsweek, "In accordance with U.S. privacy laws, ICE does not publicly discuss the administrative matters of individual employees."

The agency did not confirm or deny Shannon's claims.

Complaints Dating Back Years

Shannon says she spent years filing complaints through multiple channels. She says some went to OSC, while others were submitted to ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility and the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General.

She said her dispute with the agency began in November 2022, when she filed an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging discrimination, harassment and a hostile work environment involving her then-supervisor. She said her complaints centered on her treatment as a Black woman in the organization.

Shannon said she initially attempted to address the issues internally but believed ICE did not properly follow its procedures for handling workplace harassment.

She noted that the anti-harassment policy required reporting to a supervisor, but noted that the supervisor was the person she alleged had harassed her.

After approximately 10 months, she said the agency transferred her out of the supervisor's unit.

Emails obtained by Newsweek show that by early 2025, Shannon repeatedly asked management to intervene, objecting to reporting through her supervisor's chain of command while EEO complaints remained pending, and saying the ongoing dispute was affecting her well-being and work environment.

In a June 2025 whistleblower disclosure, Shannon alleged that agency leadership repeatedly failed to address her concerns of discrimination, harassment, and a hostile work environment. She also alleged that officials permitted her supervisor to serve in acting leadership positions despite pending EEO complaints involving him.

According to the disclosure, Shannon complained that the supervisor hung an image in a communal workspace depicting a black lion surrounded by white sheep with blue eyes, which she said she found offensive. Shannon said she viewed the image as intimidating.

"That is intimidation," Shannon said. "It makes me feel uncomfortable."

Shannon said she sought counseling and repeatedly attempted to resolve the situation internally.

Detention Concerns from ICE Officer

In a June 29, 2025, OSC disclosure, Shannon alleged that ICE's Miami Area of Responsibility had begun housing detainees overnight in temporary office space that lacked beds, showers, medical staff, and adequate emergency capabilities. She characterized the practice as an abuse of authority and named several ICE managers whom she believed were responsible.

"The facility is only authorized for short-term temporary holding, yet now being used outside it's intended and regulated purpose, placing both detainees and staff at risk of legal liability and risk," Shannon wrote in one OSC disclosure.

"It lacks the infrastructure and resources for overnight detention, placing both detainees and staff at significant risk."

Another disclosure filed on September 28 alleged that detainees were being held beyond the expiration of ICE detainers and rebooked into custody under new holds.

"It has come to my attention and direct observation that detainees—primarily female individuals—are routinely held in local custody for 72 hours or longer after the expiration of ICE detainers, in violation of federal law and established constitutional standards."

The filings show Shannon reported several concerns; however, they do not establish whether OSC substantiated them.

An ICE spokesperson said the agency is "committed to ensuring that all those in its custody reside in safe, secure, and humane environments under appropriate conditions of confinement."

"The agency takes misconduct allegations very seriously—personnel are held to the highest standards of professional and ethical behavior, and when a complaint is received, it is investigated thoroughly to determine veracity and ensure comprehensive standards are strictly maintained and enforced."

"I believe that people who violate the immigration laws, I have to deport them," she said. "But I don't have to disrespect people and violate anybody's rights doing it for statistics and for numbers."

An ICE spokesperson said the agency encourages employees and detainees to report concerns through multiple oversight channels, including the DHS Office of Inspector General, ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility and the Detention Reporting and Information Line.

Counseling and Fitness Review

In a September 2025 email complaint, Shannon said that an ICE firearms instructor called her a "crazy b****" and threatened to "let me have it" over a dispute.

On September 24, 2025, ICE issued Shannon a Letter of Counseling citing workplace incidents that the agency characterized as disruptive or unprofessional. The document says that it was not disciplinary action and would not be placed in her official personnel file. Shannon later described the counseling as retaliatory.

The dispute escalated to a fitness-for-duty review, she said.

A fitness-for-duty letter reviewed by Newsweek says that ICE sought medical information regarding Shannon's ability to perform law-enforcement duties. Separate medical documentation from a healthcare provider later said that Shannon was medically fit for duty without restrictions.

In a February 2026 retaliation complaint filed with OSC, Shannon argued that the counseling and fitness-for-duty process was initiated because she had reported misconduct through official channels.

That complaint named an acting field office director, a supervisory detention and deportation officer, and a supervisory detention and deportation officer as officials Shannon alleged were involved in retaliatory actions following her whistleblower disclosures.

Administrative Leave

Internal agency records show that Shannon was placed on paid administrative leave on February 27, 2026, for what ICE called "allegations of misconduct."

In a subsequent retaliation complaint, Shannon said the agency told her the action stemmed from allegations that she was combative, created a safety concern, and engaged in disruptive conduct during a February 26 reasonable-accommodation meeting. She denies those allegations.

Agency records show that ICE suspended her authority to carry agency-approved firearms and required her to surrender law-enforcement equipment.

A March 2 OSC filing challenged those actions and alleged that the agency removed her credentials, weapon, overtime opportunities, and operational duties because of her whistleblower activity.

In August 2026, the Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General's Whistleblower Protection Division declined to investigate Shannon's retaliation complaint and advised her to pursue the matter through OSC and other administrative channels.

Records reviewed by Newsweek show that Shannon received multiple commendations and professional recognitions during her six years with ICE, including a January 2023 commendation for border operations in Laredo, a May 2023 appreciation letter for a New Orleans assignment, a DHS leadership recognition letter and a Director's Award for Distinguished Service in 2023, as well as completion of agency mentoring and leadership-development programs in 2024 and 2025.

Surveillance Allegations Remain Unsubstantiated

Shannon also alleges that federal personnel improperly monitored her devices and private communications.

Records reviewed by Newsweek show she repeatedly reported those concerns to OPR, OIG, OSC, and local police, alleging that surveillance technology had been used against her.

She also said that co-workers repeatedly recited private home telephone conversations back to her.

"They started repeating phone conversations of mine," Shannon alleged. "Like if I would talk to my mom at home, somebody would come in and talk about something that we spoke about…and laugh in my face."

According to a July 2025 Port St. Lucie Police Department report, Shannon told officers she believed someone was illegally surveilling her cellphone and may have entered her home without permission. She reported phone issues including overheating, battery drain and unusual sounds during calls, as well as unexplained tire tracks in her garage and suspected tobacco spit at her residence.

The report documented her allegations but identified no suspect and found no evidence connecting any person to the reported incidents.

An independent forensic review of Shannon's phone found no spyware, malware, stalkerware, or unauthorized VPN. The examiner found unidentified Bluetooth records and recommended additional review, but did not determine that the device had been hacked or connect any activity to any federal agency.

Shannon also reported to police in Montgomery, Alabama, that two laptops and an iPad stored inside a signal-blocking bag were stolen from the trunk of her vehicle.

'Rights Violated'

Shannon, a breast cancer survivor who underwent surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation before joining ICE on a medical waiver, expressed frustration with her treatment.

"My rights have been egregiously violated, and after fighting for my life, this agency and its racist practices are disturbing and illegal."

"I worked really hard for this job," she said. "I don't think that these are the values and the morals and the integrity of the agency from where I started six years ago."

Shannon alleged that Black women in the agency faced harsher consequences than male colleagues accused of more serious misconduct, saying they were stripped of credentials, equipment, and workplace access over comparatively minor administrative allegations.

"The sequence and disparity raise serious concerns that administrative allegations are being used as a mechanism to discredit the reporting officer," she said, adding that the treatment sent "a chilling message to any employee who considers reporting misconduct, harassment, or discrimination within the agency."

text:
Christian Castro, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who shot a man through the door of a north Minneapolis home in January, was released Thursday evening on conditional bail from Hennepin County Jail, where he was held for state-level charges.

At his first appearance at federal district court in St. Paul on Friday for a separate case, Castro pleaded not guilty to six charges of making false statements, stemming from six alleged lies he told FBI investigators after the shooting.

Castro had appeared in state court in downtown Minneapolis Thursday to face state charges of four counts of second-degree assault as well as one count of falsely reporting a crime.

ICE agent in Jan. 14 Minneapolis shooting makes first appearance in Minnesota state court

On Jan. 14, during the peak of Operation Metro Surge, Castro engaged in a car chase with Alfredo Aljorna, ending at Aljorna’s home in north Minneapolis. Castro and another ICE agent had mistaken Aljorna for another Latino man, according to an FBI affidavit. Aljorna exited his car and slipped as he tried to get inside his house, at which point Castro attempted to arrest Aljorna. Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, Aljorna’s roommate, tried to help Aljorna, leading to an 11-second scuffle between the three. After both men escaped and ran inside, Castro shot at them with the bullet passing through the front door and hitting Sosa-Celis in the leg before coming to a stop in the wall of a child’s bedroom, according to charging documents.

In an interview in the aftermath of the shooting, Castro told an FBI agent that Sosa-Celis and Aljorna had assaulted him with a broom and a snow shovel in a three-minute fight before Castro opened fire, leading to assault charges against the two men that were dropped after surveillance footage proved Castro’s statements false.

State prosecutors charged Castro in May, and a federal grand jury indicted him in early September. An assistant U.S. attorney in Minnesota had been pursuing hefty federal civil rights charges against Castro, but was instructed by Justice Department officials in Washington, D.C. to downgrade the charges. The attorney was then fired, CBS News reported, citing four unnamed sources familiar with the matter.

The state and federal cases are taking place simultaneously. Castro, who had refused to consent to extradition to Minnesota from a Texas jail for months, turned himself in to federal authorities in early September after a federal grand jury indicted him with the six charges. He was released on bond after appearing in federal court in McAllen, Texas, and ordered to appear in federal court in Minnesota for the Friday hearing. Castro drove up to Minnesota from Texas this week, where he was arrested Wednesday in downtown Minneapolis by the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension.

On Thursday, Hennepin County District Judge Paul R. Scoggin set bail at $200,000 if Castro agrees to not possess firearms, not contact witnesses, to be electronically monitored, to sign a waiver of extradition — an agreement to be extradited without a formal hearing in the future — and to surrender his passport to state authorities immediately if he gets it back from federal authorities.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said that she expects Castro to file a motion to move the state case to federal court, which she said her office is prepared to litigate.

Castro was released on conditional bail from state custody at around 6 p.m. Thursday, according to the Hennepin County Sheriff’s jail roster. He wore a black suit and an ankle monitor to federal court Friday, a stark difference from the day prior, when he was still in state custody and appeared in state court in a glass-paneled box and an orange jail uniform.

text:
By Nate Raymond

BOSTON, Sept 18 (Reuters) – A US federal appeals court rejected on Friday a policy adopted by President Donald Trump’s administration that allows authorities to rapidly deport migrants to countries other than their own without giving them a chance to raise safety concerns.

Ruling in a case ​that is likely headed to the Supreme Court, a three-judge panel of the Boston-based 1st US ‌Circuit Court of Appeals largely upheld a February decision by a lower-court judge that declared the Department of Homeland Security’s policy unlawful.

The ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by migrants subject to deportation orders that has become a key test of what due process protections the government must provide before removing people to countries with which they have no connection.

“This decision confirms that ‌due process ​and the protections Congress enacted against persecution and torture cannot be circumvented ⁠by putting someone on a plane ⁠to a country that was never part of their removal proceedings,” Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said

Under Trump, the administration has entered into a series of agreements that have allowed it to send more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, ​in many cases Mexico, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal. Earlier in the same case, the administration twice convinced the ⁠Supreme Court to lift a preliminary injunction protecting migrants’ due process rights, clearing ⁠the way for eight men to be deported to South Sudan.

DHS had no ​immediate comment.

Under the third-country deportation program, DHS adopted a policy in March 2025 that would allow migrants to be sent to ​such countries if immigration authorities have credible diplomatic assurances they will not be persecuted ‌or tortured there.

The policy called for only minimal notice before a migrant could be sent to a third country that had not given the State Department such assurances.

THIRD COUNTRY DEPORTATIONS

US District Judge Brian Murphy, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, set aside the policy and concluded that it failed to protect migrants’ due process rights and could ⁠lead to their swift deportation to unfamiliar and potentially dangerous countries, without notice.

On appeal, the Trump administration contended that Murphy’s order if left intact would usurp its authority to execute potentially thousands of valid orders of deportation to ⁠third countries.

But US Circuit Judge Seth ‌Aframe, writing for Friday’s panel, said Murphy adopted a “sensible” interpretation of the immigration ⁠law requiring migrants be given a “meaningful” chance to raise any concerns before they ​are deported.

“DHS’s ‌proposed interpretation would deny access to that protection to a substantial swath of ​noncitizens who ⁠are sent to third countries with no notice of their destination,” Aframe wrote. “We decline to adopt such an interpretation.”

The panel included two Biden appointees, including Aframe, and a judge appointed by a Republican president.

However, the 1st Circuit overturned one part of Murphy’s ruling on procedural grounds. That part of the ruling concerned whether the government must first try to deport migrants to countries they have ties to before sending them to third countries.

(Reporting by Nate Raymond in ​Boston; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani)

description:

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed claims that ICE enforcement tactics led to reduced employment in cities where arrests spiked.

text:
Employment fell last year in U.S. cities where Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests surged the most, according to a recent study.

In cities where ICE arrests increased fastest in 2025, employment fell 0.4% below its expected trajectory both immediately after those detentions and for up to one year after a metro area was targeted, researchers with the Brookings Institution said in the report. On average, each arrest in cities where ICE's presence significantly increased was associated with four lost jobs, the nonpartisan think tank said.

"We found that employment fell in the cities where ICE activity surged, and not just among immigrants, but there were broader effects, including for Americans," Marcela Escobari, the report's lead author and a former special assistant to the White House National Security Council during the Biden administration, told CBS News.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis dismissed claims that ICE enforcement tactics led to reduced employment in cities where arrests spiked.

"The surge in illegal immigration under President Biden threatened the long-run fiscal health of the country, contributed to record high inflation and suppressed the wages of American workers," she said in a statement to CBS News. "There is no shortage of American minds and hands to grow our labor force, and President Trump's agenda to create jobs for American workers represents this Administration's commitment to capitalizing on that untapped potential while delivering on our mandate to enforce our immigration laws."

Border security has been a top priority during the second Trump administration. Stronger immigration enforcement policies "protect American workers, reduce strain on local communities, and reinforce the nation's right to control its borders and determine who enters the United States," according to a White House statement.

The Trump administration ramped up its immigration crackdown in 2025. In January, thousands of federal agents were deployed to Minneapolis-St. Paul to investigate alleged fraud, leading to mass protests and the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal officers.

In July, ICE detentions set a monthly record high for Mr. Trump's second term, with the agency taking into custody more than 46,000 individuals facing deportation because of alleged immigration violations, like entering the U.S. illegally or overstaying their visas, CBS News has reported.

Businesses disrupted

Increased ICE arrests in U.S. cities last year drove job losses in three ways, Escobari told CBS News. First, some workers stopped reporting for work because they feared encountering ICE.

"Fear drove workers to withdraw from the labor force even when they weren't arrested," she said.

This led to labor disruptions for some businesses, leading them to reduce their operating hours, delay expansion, freeze hiring, or, in some cases, lay off staff or shut down, according to Brookings.

"We spoke to people in the field who explicitly said, if their framing crew is led by immigrants and they stop working or get arrested, they can't hand off the project to their roofing crew, and the project stalls," Escobari said, referring to the impact of increased ICE enforcement in the construction sector. "The company still needs to pay its debts, and many close altogether. When they close, the project manager or equipment operator and other occupations that tend to be occupied by American workers also lose their jobs."

Rising ICE arrests in cities in 2025 also reduced employment by sapping consumer demand and spending, hurting local businesses, according to the Brookings researchers.

"These [ICE] operations engender widespread fear, and when people stop going out, they stop spending, and that forces businesses to close," Escobari said.

Other research has also found a negative impact of increased ICE enforcement on local economies. A 2026 study from the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania found that economic activity and consumer spending dropped last year in metro areas where ICE conducted raids.

"Effects intensify near raid sites, do not dissipate over time and are remarkably general: Declines occur regardless of neighborhood demography, affect workplaces and consumer-facing stores across myriad industries, and trigger no substitution to online shopping," Exequiel Hernandez, an expert on global and corporate strategy, wrote. "The breadth of the local economic damage mirrors the breadth of the enforcement approach."

text:
Staring into the camera, Rep. Maria Salazar cut a new campaign ad that told President Trump what so many of her fellow Hispanic Republicans in Miami are saying: Immigration crackdown has gone too far.

Why it matters: The anger at Trump over heavy-handed immigration enforcement is palpable in Miami-Dade County, and there's mounting political worry among Republicans across the state that it could cost the GOP in the midterm elections.

Zoom in: A bellwether, Miami-Dade is Florida's most-populous county, which Trump flipped to the Republican column in 2020 and 2024 thanks to strong Latino support, especially among Cuban Americans.

"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says in her ad. "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

Trump carried her district by 15 points two years ago. Today, she's tied in polls with newscaster Eliot Rodriguez, a fellow Cuban American, who criticized her for voting to approve Trump's immigration crackdown in the first place.

A Trump adviser told Axios: "I'm getting the Trumpiest Cubans sending me videos from Miami of guys getting busted at places like the gas station, for no apparent reason."

By the numbers: In Miami-Dade, 62% of the county's 1.3 million registered voters are Hispanic. They account for 76% of the registered Republicans.

63% of Hispanic voters said they supported "deporting illegal immigrants" while 34% were opposed to them, according to a poll conducted last month by a GOP pollster and shared with Axios

But those numbers switched when it came to how deportations were being carried out: Just 29% were in favor; 58% were opposed.

"The support is just evaporating. The economy sucks and ICE is just out of control," said the pollster, who's from Miami. "People feel they didn't sign up for this."

Yes, but: Trump ran on a platform of mass deportations. He promised to target undocumented criminals, but the president's critics warned that his aggressive immigration push would lead to raids, arrests in the streets, racial profiling and separated families.

"There was truth in advertising," the pollster said.

Trump last year also began revoking Temporary Protected Status for as many as 1.3 million people across the country, some of whom first received the TPS designation in 1998.

"Temporary means temporary," a White House official told Axios, noting that President Biden had allowed millions into the country under TPS and a new program that Trump reversed.

Ground zero for the Miami-Dade fear and loathing is in Doral. Trump owns a prized golf course there. It's also nicknamed "Doralzuela" because of the large Venezuelan population.

Businesses were hit doubly hard last year when Trump canceled TPS for Venezuelans: Legal workers lost the authorization to work, once-legal residents fled, and those who are still there are in hiding or constantly getting picked up by federal agents.

"Our sales have dropped 70%. We spend hours empty," Katia Rios of Pipo Burgers, told CBS Miami on Wednesday.

Doral Mayor Christi Fraga, a Republican, has been besieged with complaints and has tried to distance herself from the Trump administration. "I don't agree with the way things are handled," she told CBS.

Zoom out: Salazar's Republican congressional colleague from Miami, Mario Diaz-Balart, has a district that stretches from Doral on Florida's southeast coast to Naples on its southwest coast.

"We've been sending this message to the administration for months," he said of Salazar's ad. Diaz-Balart, however, hasn't spoken publicly against the administration because he prefers to work behind the scenes.

Republicans say they're not too worried about conservative Hispanic voters switching to vote for Democrats, but they all believe turnout for the GOP will be low, which could affect legislative and congressional contests, and perhaps the race for governor.

"Byron Donalds better watch out," a top Republican consultant said of the Republican congressman locked in a tighter-than-expected gubernatorial race against Democrat David Jolly. (A Donalds spokesman said Jolly will lose.)

Friction point: Miami's best-known Cuban American political figure, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, has been publicly supportive of the administration's immigration policies, despite the outcry back home.

Rubio was identified with bipartisan immigration reform in 2013, when he served in the Senate.

Venezuelans have grown increasingly agitated with Rubio and Trump for not voicing support for an election date in Venezuela and for the administration's transactional relationship with its acting president, Delcy Rodriguez, a socialist who came to power after the U.S. ousted strongman Nicolas Maduro on Jan. 3.

"There's a growing feeling that Trump just wanted our oil," a Venezuelan Republican activist said.

Between the lines: Miami-Dade has one of the country's most-diverse Latino populations. Cuban Americans are the dominant group, but there are sizable communities with roots elsewhere in Latin America.

Cuban Americans tend to be the most conservative because of the exile community that swelled after Fidel Castro took power there in the 1959 revolution.

Exiles from families who fled leftist oppression or violence in Nicaragua, Colombia and Venezuela also found common cause with Cuban-American Republicans over the years.

Now, these South Florida Hispanic communities are grappling with an immigration system that treats them about the same as Haitians in Miami or arrivals from Mexico in more liberal U.S. cities such as Los Angeles.

Cubans once enjoyed expansive immigration protections in the U.S.

Under Trump, they're being deported in large numbers to Mexico and even countries in Africa.

Behind the scenes: Salazar's broadside against Trump followed days of discussions between her office, Diaz-Balart's and the administration over the arrest of Luis Galeano, a Nicaraguan journalist in Miami with an active asylum application.

The Department of Homeland Security accused Galeano of overstaying his visa.

The lawmakers say his visa should have been paused because of his asylum claim, which stemmed from his critical coverage of Nicaragua's leftist dictator, Daniel Ortega, who confiscated Galeano's property and stripped him of Nicaraguan citizenship.

"There has got to be a better way to do this," Diaz-Balart said. "I'm hearing that everywhere."

text:
WASHINGTON—Yesterday, Representative James R. Walkinshaw (D-VA), Representative James P. McGovern (D-MA), Ranking Member of the House Rules Committee and the Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC), along with Senators Jeff Merkley (D-OR) and Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), sent a letter to Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling on the Trump Administration to protect people who have fled repression in China and could face persecution or torture if they are sent back.

McGovern, Merkley, Duckworth, and Walkinshaw all serve on the CECC—a congressional commission that monitors and documents human rights violations in the People’s Republic of China (PRC).

In the letter, the lawmakers called on the U.S. government to stop the practice of detaining at-risk individuals, release those currently in detention, prohibit them from being deported to the PRC, and give fair and timely consideration of their applications for asylum.

“Many people who have fled persecution in the PRC come to the United States with an expectation that they can find refuge,” the Members wrote. “They should be given every opportunity to apply for asylum if they have not yet done so and given fair and timely consideration of such application for asylum or other protection. Under no circumstances should at-risk individuals be deported to the PRC.”

The Members also made the letter public so immigration attorneys and advocates can use it in cases involving Uyghurs, Hong Kongers, Tibetans and others who fear persecution if returned to China.

“There are likely many more detainees at ICE facilities, perhaps lacking representation, who fear deportation to a country run by a government that seeks to do them harm,” the Members continued. “There are perhaps others who have already been sent back to the PRC who are now experiencing persecution, torture or worse. Thus, we see value in making this letter and its message public.”

The letter notes that the U.S. government deporting an individual to a country where their life or freedom would be threatened (also known as “refoulement”) would violate both United States and international law, and would also be a betrayal of that promise by then-Senator Marco Rubio to provide refuge to those subject to the repression of the Chinese Communist Party, when he introduced the Hong Kong Safe Harbor Act and the Uyghur Human Rights Protection Act.

The full text of the letter is available here.

text:
Revealed: ICE Lost Count of Miscarriages, While Detaining a Record Number of Pregnant Women

ICE is arresting a record number of pregnant women and teenagers – placing them in detention centers where they say it can be exceedingly difficult to access medical care. ICE recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration, the documents show, but the agency has no data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025. Meanwhile, detained pregnant women report that they are struggling to access routine and emergency medical care.

The Trump Administration Shut Down a Police Misconduct Database. Now It’s Facing a FOIA Lawsuit

Last year the Trump administration shut down a national database of misconduct by federal law enforcement officers. A coalition of civil rights and police accountability groups filed a FOIA lawsuit on September 4 after waiting 10 months for the Department of Justice (DOJ) to release records about why it pulled the plug on the National Law Enforcement Accountability Database (NLEAD), a nonpublic database tracking misconduct by federal law enforcement officers.

Zambia: By Cancelling Passports, Authorities Are Using Administrative Powers to Silence Critics

Amnesty International has documented a rapid deterioration in the human rights situation in the country in the run-up to, during and after the general elections, marked by arbitrary arrests and detention, as well as attacks and intimidation targeting human rights defenders, activists, journalists and opposition political party members. As electoral tensions intensified, these violations were followed by further arrests of opposition members. On 11 September, the Zambian authorities issued a notice cancelling passports belonging to several government critics “in the interest of national security.”

Latin America Accounted for 85% of Environmental Defender Killings in 2025, Report Says

At least 124 land and environmental defenders were killed around the world last year, with Latin America accounting for 85% of the deaths as conflicts over land and natural resources continued to put Indigenous people and small-scale farmers at risk, according to a report released Wednesday. The annual report by environmental and human rights advocacy group Global Witness documented 105 killings in Latin America in 2025. Colombia was the deadliest country for the fourth consecutive year, with 39 killings, followed by Brazil with 26.

text:
Outside the immigrant detention center in Tacoma on Wednesday, Humphrey Oyoo was trying to find his pregnant wife.

Cece Mokua, 29, had been detained the day before, while going to what was supposed to be an interview for her asylum application with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services – an agency that under past administrations was not involved with immigration enforcement and instead focused on adjudicating applications for legal status.

Instead, Mokua found herself dealing with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, who separated her from Oyoo and their 1-year-old, kept her for hours in a holding cell and took her to the Northwest ICE Processing Center.

But when Oyoo tried to leave a message for his wife Wednesday at the front desk of the Tacoma detention center, he was told she had been released. But had she really? Or was she being transferred to another ICE facility out of state? That has been happening to hundreds of people recently, and they too had usually been listed in the detention center’s system as “released.”

The front-desk officer couldn’t tell him.

About an hour later, Mokua called her husband. She truly was being released, but would remain in just-initiated deportation proceedings. He could pick her up in Tukwila.

So ended a confusing two-day ordeal for the couple, highlighting the unpredictability of current immigration enforcement tactics and the difficulty of getting information about people who have been detained. For a pregnant woman such as Mokua, the experience can be especially difficult. Mokua is five months pregnant and said she experienced contractions and a migraine while detained.

Supporters of the couple, including members of the activist group Defend Migrants Alliance who were at the detention center Wednesday with Oyoo, believe Mokua walked into a trap: a supposed asylum interview that was a pretext for her arrest.

“We have seen from time to time people called in for appointments with USCIS that really ended up being appointments for ICE to either arrest or initiate removal proceedings,” Matt Adams, legal director of the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project, said by email.

While not the norm, such ICE arrests across the country make it impossible to advise people on whether they might be detained in any particular situation, said Andrea Sáenz, a former member of the federal government’s Board of Immigration Appeals now working at Co-Counsel NYC, a New York-based legal services group.

The majority of people arrested by ICE locally and nationally in recent months have no criminal record. But someone who does, despite how old the charges or their level of severity, faces an increased risk of enforcement.

Mokua on New Year’s Day 2024 was charged with driving while under the influence, later amended to reckless driving, a gross misdemeanor. She said she was driving through fog on the wrong side of the road and crashed into the median when an oncoming car approached. She served no jail time, according to court records.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not provide answers this week to questions about Mokua’s arrest and detention.

A previous U.S. Department of Homeland Security statement commented generally on the detention of people with pending asylum applications, which was fairly unusual under past administrations. “To be clear, a pending application does NOT confer legal status in the United States. Any application for asylum does not preclude immigration enforcement,” the statement said.

ICE last month detained Kenyan physician and asylum applicant Robert Sidhe as he was returning to his Lynnwood home from the gym. In Seattle, he has worked as a patient care technician, assisting nurses, at UW Medicine. A federal judge ordered him released.

After Mokua’s arrest, SEIU 775 expressed concern about ICE enforcement against healthcare workers. Mokua does not work in healthcare, but her husband is a home healthcare aide and SEIU union member in Spokane, where the couple lives. He also runs an adult family home for seniors and others who can’t live on their own.

“We are already facing a shortage of caregivers as the population ages, and attacking immigrants will only deepen that shortage and make it harder for residents to get the care they need,” the union said in a statement.

According to Mokua, she came to the U.S. legally as a 15-year-old to live with an aunt in New Jersey and to escape female genital mutilation, a standard practice of her tribe. She finished high school in New Jersey and then college, majoring in biology, she said.

The aunt was supposed to make sure her young charge’s visa was renewed but would get irritated when Mokua asked about it. “So I stopped asking her,” Mokua said. Her visa expired.

From Kenya, her dad advised Mokua to apply for an internship anyway. Her employer would likely help her fix her status, her dad thought. But Mokua said she was distracted by college life and some difficult experiences that affected her mental health. She had a brief, unhappy marriage after college to a U.S. citizen who promised to help her achieve legal status but never did, Mokua said.

She moved to Spokane, where she has relatives, and several years ago met Oyoo on a dating app. They knew a lot of the same people. Oyoo, who said he is a green-card holder, is also from Kenya and lived for a time in New Jersey.

They had a baby, Josiah, and a month ago married. Meanwhile, Mokua said, she applied for asylum on the basis of her tribe’s female genital mutilation practices.

The family showed up to the scheduled USCIS interview with supporters who had invited the press to come. ICE had previously arrested at least a handful of Kenyans, they said, creating foreboding.

Oyoo and a recent law school grad accompanying them trailed behind Mokua as they went through the security line to get into the Department of Homeland Security’s regional headquarters in Tukwila. Mokua was focused on getting to the 7:30 a.m. appointment on time.

Oyoo had the baby and stroller, slowing him down. He handed the baby to the law school grad as he went through security and by the time he turned around, his wife was nowhere to be seen.

“Where did she go?” he thought.

He and the law school grad went to a second-floor waiting room. “By the time we were getting to the fifth hour, I knew there’s something wrong,” Oyoo recalled. He eventually got to an ICE officer to ask what was happening and was given a non-answer. He would have to wait for her call.

Mokua had been immediately approached by an officer, she said later. He led her up stairs to a waiting area and, in a few minutes, she was called into another room. This is her interview, she thought. But when the door opened, she saw two officers in ICE uniforms who told her she was under arrest.

She protested that she was there for an asylum interview and that her husband, child and lawyer were nearby. (The law school graduate was there for moral support, not to represent her.) But they pulled her arms behind her back, handcuffed her and took her through what she described as a back door. She did not tell them she was pregnant.

“I was scared and nervous,” she said.

She was taken to see an ICE officer, who began asking her when she had come to the U.S and why she fell out of status.

Then, Mokua said, she was placed in a cold, bare holding cell with concrete benches. She was offered noodle soup in a cup but turned it down. She had lost her appetite.

She stayed there until about 8 p.m., she said, as ICE arrested roughly 15 more people. They were men and were put in a separate holding cell. Eventually, ICE officers loaded them all onto a bus – chained and cuffed around their hands, waist and ankles – and took them to the detention center.

Mokua said the holding cell she went into there was even worse: “filthy, smaller.” Another long wait began while ICE processed what she said were some 30 people just arrested.

She said the only drinking water was from a sink above the toilet and she worried that was unsanitary. So she didn’t drink at all. The migraine and contractions started.

At that point, she made detention center officials aware of her condition and saw a detention center nurse. He didn’t give her any medicine, she said, but wrote a note saying she should have a bottom bunk when she got to her dormlike unit, making it easier to maneuver.

She reached the unit about 8 a.m., she said. The beds came with thin mattresses and no pillows, she said. The food served was cold and looked unappetizing. Again, she passed on eating. But there were books and games available as well as companionship with people from all over world.

She had a video call with her husband and Josiah. The 1-year-old cried.

By 12:45 p.m., she was told, without explanation, she was being released. She wondered if it was because officials realized she was pregnant.

The Trump administration has knowingly detained pregnant immigrants, disregarding a Biden-era policy. But the current administration has faced criticism for doing so and, after 18 miscarriages by detained pregnant women, has stopped tracking that figure, The Guardian reported this month.

Officers took Mokua back to the Homeland Security regional headquarters and then to a nearby building that houses a program ICE uses to monitor people in deportation proceedings who are not detained.

She came out with a watch monitor and a small bag of belongings, looking dazed. She wore a long, yellow sweater coat over her detention center uniform: a navy sweatshirt and sweatpants. Oyoo drove up with Josiah and she embraced her husband, then swooped Josiah into her arms.

Oyoo suggested they go to an Indian restaurant to get his wife’s favorite food. She hadn’t eaten in two days at this point.

The air was celebratory but Mokua’s mind was still on what lay ahead: a Monday check-in with ICE in Spokane. She didn’t think she could handle another surprise detention.
