name: Human Rights
title: Held in hotels or detained for a year after being deported to Africa: 'This is called human trafficking'
description:
All the deported migrants this newspaper spoke with were first held in U.S. detention centers; none were notified they would be transferred to Africa, and none signed consent forms.
They were being deported despite having a “stay of removal,” a form of protection in the United States.
Yet when the ICE plane touched down again, they were actually in Equatorial Guinea.
At the Hotel Bamy in Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea, the deportees are staying.
Yet neither the United States nor the African countries are carrying out that personalized assessment.
text:
Among so many faces, Roberto Mosquera remembered one in particular the day he arrived in Eswatini, a small country tucked away in southern Africa. He kept seeing that face over the following 14 months, which passed slowly and unbearably in the compressed world between the white and gray walls of the maximum-security cell at Matsapha prison. The man is serious, tall, dark-skinned and wears round glasses. His name is Jabulani Kunene and he is the prison official in charge. For more than a year, Mosquera has asked him the same question every time he passes by: “How long are you going to keep me locked up here?” Kunene has always given him the same answer: “I don’t know, Roberto, I don’t know.”

Mosquera no longer calls his cell a cell; he calls it “the little house.” He bought a coffee maker with money sent by his family in Miami; he bought a single-burner stove to fry eggs or reheat soup; there is always a bottle of liquid bleach to clean the bathroom, razors, and bottles of shampoo, because you can be imprisoned, he thinks, but you should not be left to rot. “I like to dress well, go to Miami restaurants with my daughters; I am a city man,” he says during a video call, where he sports an immaculate beard, gold-capped teeth, a high-carat chain, a blue cap and a gray pullover — not the inmate uniform they dressed him in the day he arrived handcuffed at the feet and hands, when he was given a tag with a number on the front and asked to look at the camera so they could take his prison mugshot.

If Mosquera is not wearing an inmate uniform today, it is because of everything he has resisted in recent months, since U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained him at one of his immigration appointments, locked him in the Krome detention center, transferred him to an airport in Texas and deported him without his consent to southern Africa. Since then dozens of people have been sent to that continent after the U.S. signed multimillion-dollar agreements with nearly 14 African countries. The flights operated by ICE mostly depart from Alexandria Airport in Louisiana or from Texas and land over 20 hours later. The mechanism so far has always been the same: no migrant knows where they are being deported to until they step onto unknown soil.

Through a 30-day hunger strike and several arguments with officers, Mosquera has won small freedoms amid his long confinement: permission to wear his own clothes, access to an interior yard from his cell, escorted trips to buy food at a nearby shop, and the right for himself and others to have cellphones to speak with family. Those are a lot of concessions for a prisoner, but none are enough for him, at 59, a father of four daughters, whom the Donald Trump administration called a “depraved monster” and expelled from the country even though he had long since served his sentence.

From Texas he was put on a flight that, because of its duration, could not be going to Cuba — the country where he was born and which has refused to take him back for nearly three decades — nor to Mexico, where so many migrants have been landing lately. Another detainee, using gestures, asked during the journey where on earth they thought they were taking them. Mosquera drew a circle with his hands in the air. He wanted to say they would likely end up on the other side of the world.

Over several weeks, EL PAÍS spoke by video call with a dozen migrants from Cuba, Honduras, Brazil, and Colombia who have been deported to countries such as Liberia, the Central African Republic, Eswatini, or Equatorial Guinea and who remain today in an indecipherable legal limbo.

No one, not even lawyers, knows how to untangle the migratory knot they are in. “These people risk being legally trapped between three states: the United States says its responsibility ended with the expulsion; the African receiving state may not grant them any lasting immigration or protection status; and their countries of origin may be places where international law prohibits their return,” explained Michael Gyan Nyarko, executive director of the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa (IHRDA). The concern now, according to Gyan Nyarko, lies in how the White House is using deportations to third countries to secure, indirectly, what is unlawful within the United States.

All the deported migrants this newspaper spoke with were first held in U.S. detention centers; none were notified they would be transferred to Africa, and none signed consent forms. Some were pursuing asylum cases; others had been granted protection by U.S. immigration judges under the Convention Against Torture (CAT).

Colombian Arín García Yepes, who arrived in Liberia on an ICE-operated flight from Louisiana on August 20, still recalls the moment they were about to board the plane and asked one another: “Do you have withholding of removal?” “Are you protected in this country?” Like him, almost everyone answered yes. They were being deported despite having a “stay of removal,” a form of protection in the United States.

They are now held in maximum-security prisons or remain in hotels under the supervision of African authorities. So far, none of the people interviewed had documentation or identification allowing them to stay or move about legally and safely in those countries — some of which have authoritarian governments, others internal civil wars. When the African night falls and they rest their heads on pillows, all these people ask themselves again and again: Is the treatment we are receiving legal? What will happen to us next?

Savi Arvey, director of refugee and immigrant rights policy at Human Rights First, an organization that tracks these deportations, said these transfers to third countries — which she calls “illegal deportations” — are part of the broader Trump administration effort “to undermine the global protection system and make countries around the world accomplices in its mass deportation campaign.”

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is deporting migrants who not only did not identify those African countries as possible destinations during their immigration procedures, but many were also protected against removal orders. The Trump administration is also using these deportation agreements to dispose of pending asylum cases in its courts.

“Most of these Latin Americans sent to African countries had been deemed by U.S. immigration judges to be people who would face persecution or torture if returned to their countries of origin, and they had been granted protection,” Arvey says. “Now the United States is evading its international legal obligations by sending these refugees to third countries, where they have been arbitrarily imprisoned, left in indefinite legal limbo, or returned to the very dangers they fled.”

When asked about the guarantees and protections for migrants deported to African countries, a State Department spokesperson said the U.S. government “will use every legal means at its disposal to remove those who do not have a right to remain in our country.” “As Secretary [Marco] Rubio has stated, our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and to strengthen United States border security is unwavering,” the spokesperson added.

The migration and legal limbo

Arístides Fernández García, 37, answers the call from his room at Maison Confort, an apartment lodging in Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic, where several migrants are staying. He had never committed any crime or done anything that, in anyone’s eyes, made him a criminal. Until now he had remained in the United States with I-220A status, the same status that has prevented the legalization of more than 500,000 Cubans like him, and he was detained on the day he appeared before a judge in the immigration court in Miami. The first time Fernández spoke with EL PAÍS, a few days had passed since his arrival in Africa on July 31, handcuffed at the feet and hands on a multi-hour flight carrying about 80 people detained by ICE.

More than 40 days have passed and García speaks to this newspaper again. To date, no authority has approached them to explain what plan, if any, they have for them. “An animal has more rights than we do; this is called human trafficking, they have us kidnapped in this country, we have no papers, we are at the mercy of whatever may happen,” García says.

Other migrants interviewed said they were in the same situation. They live on the food provided at the centers, have no passports, receive no guidance, and some report suffering malaria or stomach illnesses; others have been taken to hospital in emergencies, and many find it difficult to communicate in English or French. Organizations working on the ground have documented that several have been beaten or threatened at gunpoint.

To leave Maison Confort — whether to go to the barber, the market, or to walk minimally around Bangui — Yasmani Noel Moreno de Armas, a 31-year-old Cuban who was detained in May 2025 during a beach outing in Florida, pays the hotel security guards two or three dollars. Even so, when they are seen on the street, the local police always stop them. “They told us we could no longer walk the streets,” he says. Apparently they are not detained in the same way as the migrants sent to Eswatini, but they remain under the control and at the disposal of Liberian authorities.

Recently Moreno contacted a representative of the Cuban embassy in Congo to ask what solutions were available for them. “They told me I could not return to Cuba, that Cuba does not want me; they said because I was a rafters migrant, to keep trying in the future.” The diplomat promised to help and said she would follow up, but she has not replied to any further messages. The hotel houses Afghan, Vietnamese, and Russian migrants, and some are known to have been at the facility for a year. The big question García and De Armas ask is whether time will stretch out the same way for them.

From Liberia, Honduran William Ortiz Hernández is no less anguished. He was deported on a flight that left Alexandria on August 20 with about 20 people, despite a U.S. judge years earlier granting him CAT protection, meaning the government could not send him back to his home country. As such, he was deported to a completely unrelated country. When he learned he was in a place called Liberia, he grabbed a phone provided by the authorities and typed into Google: L I B E R I A. The search results and the little he has since seen told him he is “in a very poor country. Women have approached me with their children, very needy, and I would like to have money to help these people.” At the Creed Lodge, the hotel in Monrovia where they have been housed, he has received treatment for his diabetes; he says there has been no shortage of food and they were given some clothing. Over the days they were also issued an ID that only serves to withdraw money sent by family via Western Union. But it is not enough.

“I was not hiding from immigration in the United States. Why are they taking me out now and not telling me which country I’m going to?” he asks. “Here I am without an ID; I don’t go outside; I am afraid. We met with the government and they warned us how dangerous this is. We feel stressed, we feel very confused because we are in a country where we know neither the language nor anything. I feel like they dumped me in a trash heap.”

The day Hernández got off the ICE flight that delivered them, five migrants refused with all their strength to descend the plane’s stairs. “We told them we didn’t feel safe, but they forced us to get off. They carried me between four people and beat me while I was handcuffed,” Cuban Carlos Rodríguez told EL PAÍS a few days after being deported. With him were three other Cubans and a Brazilian, whom authorities promised that if they stayed calm they would return them to the United States. Yet when the ICE plane touched down again, they were actually in Equatorial Guinea. “How can a government, in the space of a few hours, send us to another country, and that country accept us?” Rodríguez asks. “This is human trafficking, they trafficked us on a plane.”

EL PAÍS tried to contact the migrants sent to Equatorial Guinea again; some had serious medical conditions, but family members confirmed that authorities had taken away their phones so they could not file complaints with the press. “I haven’t heard from him in a week; they have cut them off,” said Caridad, the mother of Leonardo Sánchez, a Cuban deported to that country with a large abdominal hernia and an operation pending. “What they’re doing is criminal; the treatment is unfair,” his mother complained from Miami.

At the Hotel Bamy in Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea, the deportees are staying. Lawyer F. — who asked not to be identified because the government of that country is retaliating against lawyers who, like him, want to represent the deportees — brought sanitary pads for women, toothbrushes for everyone, and some medicines that the authorities had not provided.

“There are people with diabetes, high blood pressure or cardiovascular diseases receiving very poor medical care, because the nurse cannot give them any medication,” he says. “We are surprised that there are several people with very dangerous medical conditions, and we are concerned that the United States is including them on deportation lists.”

Those who ended up in Equatorial Guinea are, like those sent to other countries, without any form of identification, visa, travel document or safe-conduct, EG JUSTICE director Tutu Alicante — a Guinean lawyer who works with deportees to that country — confirmed. “In practice they are undocumented: they have no legal status, no pathway to regularize their presence and there is no formal timeline for their release or expulsion.” That, according to Alicante, is the core of the legal limbo in which they find themselves: “They fall outside both asylum/immigration frameworks and any criminal process, and remain detained at the discretion of the government of Equatorial Guinea, an authoritarian government that does not respect the rule of law.”

Opacity of agreements

On March 15, 2025, with images of dozens of Venezuelans disembarking from a plane at the CECOT mega-prison in El Salvador, a new chapter began in the history of Trump-era mass deportations after the government invoked the Foreign Enemies Act. The following month, a judge ordered a suspension of these deportations until the U.S. Supreme Court issued a ruling to resume expulsions of migrants to third countries. Since then, the NGO Third Country Deportation Watch has recorded more than 23,000 people sent to some 35 countries, operations in which the U.S. government has invested more than $49 million in funding.

At least 14 African countries are willing to receive migrants: Burundi, Cameroon, Cape Verde, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini, Ghana, Liberia, Libya, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, South Sudan and Uganda. All have signed bilateral agreements, or what are called “verbal notes,” which so far remain opaque. In diplomatic exchanges, the African governments commit to receive migrants sent from the United States but do not specify what benefits they receive in return. EL PAÍS obtained the repatriation agreements with the Central African Republic (which received $85 million in U.S. government funds), Equatorial Guinea (which received $7.5 million) and Liberia (which obtained $5 million to manage the reception of migrants).

The agreements state that the U.S. government has at least seven days before the deportation flight to notify the receiving government of the list of people to be transferred, and that each country is free to accept or reject the deportees. Some reserve the right to deport these migrants onward to other countries. The documents also include diplomatic assurances regarding compliance with obligations under the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees and the Convention Against Torture, under which they agree not to persecute or torture any third-country national sent by the United States and not to send such nationals to any other country where they might be persecuted or tortured. Nevertheless, some observers have raised alarms about violations of these commitments.

“We know that, in practice, these assurances are not being upheld,” says Yael Schacher, director for the Americas and Europe at Refugees International. “Many countries that have signed agreements including such diplomatic assurances — among them Ghana and Equatorial Guinea — are detaining and mistreating people they receive from the United States and have no selection mechanism to ensure they do not repatriate third-country nationals to places where they will be persecuted.”

Schacher says U.S. law — as well as compliance with the UN Refugee Convention and the Convention Against Torture — requires an individualized assessment to determine whether a person is likely to suffer harm or be tortured if deported to certain places. Yet neither the United States nor the African countries are carrying out that personalized assessment.

The last recourse for lawyers and organizations has been to sue some African governments. After six people in Equatorial Guinea were forcibly sent to their countries of origin, a group of organizations filed a complaint with the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights on behalf of 14 expelled people who had been granted international protection by the United States. Many people are concerned about what they call “chain deportation,” which occurs when the United States transfers a migrant to an African third-country, and that country in turn returns the migrant to the very country from which they had sought protection.

“The deportees have confidentially told us that law enforcement officials have said they will all be forced to return to their countries of origin,” says Gyan Nyarko of IHRDA, which represents some cases. “Therefore, it does not appear that the government of Equatorial Guinea intends to honor the agreement it signed with the United States, including the commitment to grant legal status to the deportees. The United States also shares responsibility in this situation, since authorities were informed of the government of Equatorial Guinea’s conduct toward the deportees and yet no action is being taken.”

Time passes more slowly and feels heavier than ever for everyone. Every so often, the guards at Matsapha Prison approach Roberto Mosquera and talk about what they each know about the places they come from. Sometimes the guards burst out laughing. “I tell them, ‘I had no idea what Africa was like; I’d only seen it in movies — tigers, lions, giraffes.’” The guards find it funny, but in reality, the story hides a truth: that Mosquera should never have landed, the way he did, in a place called Eswatini. “My mistakes are done; I can’t change them, but I was able to change my life,” he says. “I don’t want to stay in this country; I’m not African; this isn’t my culture. I want to be transferred to the United States so they can give me due process.”

From another cell, Jamaican pastor Junior Alves, a 64-year-old man who was also sent to Eswatini, said: “Not only have I been deported, but I’ve also been imprisoned. For what reason?” About 2,300 miles away, in Bangui, Arístides Fernández García still can’t believe it: “What am I doing in Africa? Why did I, who wanted to live the American dream, have to pay the price for this?” And elsewhere in Liberia, William Ortiz Hernández lives in fear that one day he’ll be sent back to Honduras. There, a group of men killed his cousin, then his uncle. Nothing suggests that he won’t be next.

text:
A federal appeals court ruled Friday that immigrants facing deportation to third countries must be given sufficient notice before being sent to nations where they have no ties.

The unanimous decision by a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit struck down a Department of Homeland Security policy that allowed the swift deportation of immigrants to third countries.

"An individual's right to contest removal to a country based on a fear of persecution in that country means little if one does not receive prior notice of the intended removal destination and a meaningful opportunity to contest that destination," wrote Circuit Judge Seth Aframe.

The ruling on Friday allows migrants to contest deportations to countries other than their place of origin.

According to the lawsuit, immigrants were routinely transferred to third countries with little to no notice when the administration cited "diplomatic assurances" that the receiving nation would not mistreat them.

ABC News previously interviewed a group of Latin American men who were deported to the Central African Republic and were not informed of their destination until several hours into the flight.

"I feel kidnapped," one of the men, Aristides Fernandez Garcia, said. "They have violated all the rights that exist in life, because we are human beings."

In recent months, the administration has expanded third-country deportations after securing formal deals with 35 countries, including Liberia, Ghana, the Central African Republic and Sierra Leone.

Savi Arvey, director of policy for refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, said the U.S. has spent nearly $50 million on these deportation agreements.

"I think the fact that the administration is sending refugees to the most dangerous countries in the world, to countries run by corrupt autocrats where they've been arbitrarily detained and sent back to persecution and torture, shows that the administration has a complete disregard for due process, for international law and for human dignity," Arvey said.

text:
Geoff Bennett:

Less than a year ago, aggressive immigration raids in Democratic-led cities were drawing national headlines and sparking protests across the country. But in recent months, the Trump administration has shifted its approach.

Instead of relying as heavily on high-profile enforcement operations, federal immigration authorities are increasingly working with state and local police, especially in Republican-led states. And the result is what some immigration advocates have called a shadow surge, a quieter form of enforcement that has helped drive ICE arrests to record levels, often with far less public attention.

To help us understand what's happening, we're joined now by Lauren Villagran, a reporter with The Marshall Project. She was part of a team that analyzed ICE data obtained by the Deportation Data Project at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA.

Thanks for being with us.

Lauren Villagran, The Marshall Project:

Thanks for having me.

Geoff Bennett:

So, not long ago, immigration enforcement was highly visible. There were those major operations in Minneapolis and in Chicago. Now arrests are rising, but the approach is less conspicuous.

What changed?

Lauren Villagran:

Yes, I mean, I think for many Americans, the mass deportation campaign of President Donald Trump has largely faded into the background without these sort of in-your-face operations that we saw earlier this year in Chicago, Minneapolis, Los Angeles, et cetera.

But the reality is that, even though you're seeing fewer headlines, the number of immigration arrests has risen dramatically across the country. Especially over the summer, we saw a massive uptick in arrests and the highest level ever in August.

Geoff Bennett:

So where are these arrests increasing, and why?

Lauren Villagran:

Yes, so, this year, we've seen immigration arrests more than double in 15 states and Washington, D.C. I mean, there are the usual suspects like Texas and Florida, which have long been top enforcers for the Trump administration's mass deportation program.

But we're also seeing pretty dramatic increases in communities across the country. Geoff, one of the things we have seen is more than 2,000 agreements between state and local law enforcement to conduct immigration stops.

Geoff Bennett:

And what does that look like in practice, these agreements with these state and local law enforcement agencies that have now a hand in immigration enforcement?

Lauren Villagran:

Yes, so it looks different in different states.

For example, in Republican-led Florida, you have got the Florida State Highway Patrol conducting immigration stops and handing thousands of immigrants stopped for minor traffic violations over to ICE. And then you have got enforcement like we see in Butler County, Ohio, where a single sheriff's department has 44 deputies trained and deputized to conduct ICE-style arrests and hand immigrants over to ICE.

You know, that's a quarter of the force in this particular town. States like Ohio and Missouri don't represent a majority of the arrests, but you have seen a really dramatic increase. Ohio, at the end of the Biden administration, had just 20 of these agreements with the federal government to conduct immigration stops. Today, they have 20.

In Missouri, that number is 130. So the enforcement has been less covered by the national media, in part because it's happening on the backs of state and local law enforcement. It's hard to know when it's a traffic stop and when it's an immigration stop.

Geoff Bennett:

And that's by design? The administration wanted the same results without the level of public confrontation and public attention.

Lauren Villagran:

So you saw President Trump fire Border Patrol commander at large Greg Bovino earlier this year, as well as Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

When the new homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, came in, he promised results without the headlines. And that's what we have seen over the past six months. So, while many Americans may not be paying as much attention, given the enforcement style, immigrant communities are feeling it.

Geoff Bennett:

There's also the question, Lauren, of who is being arrested. The administration makes the case that these deportees, that these detainees have criminal records. What does the data actually show?

Lauren Villagran:

Right. We keep hearing that phrase the worst of the worst.

The reality is -- and this data has been pretty consistent over the past year -- that, in a snapshot in July, when there were more than 65,000 people detained, 70 percent had no criminal conviction.

Geoff Bennett:

And while we have you, Lauren, late this afternoon, federal appeals court rejected the president's third-country deportation policy.

Quickly, remind us what that is. This will certainly be appealed, but bring us up to speed.

Lauren Villagran:

Right.

So this isn't just a Trump administration thing. We'd seen this previously in past administrations, where the executive branch would strike an agreement with a so-called third country, when, for example, nationals of countries where it's hard to deport people like China or Cuba or Venezuela, they would potentially send those detainees to another country like Mexico or Ecuador.

The difference now is that the Trump administration has struck dozens of these deals and sent nearly 30,000 people to a country that isn't the country they came from. That's according to Human Rights First.

Geoff Bennett:

Lauren Villagran, reporter with The Marshall Project, thanks again for your time this evening.

Lauren Villagran:

Thank you.

text:
(CN) — Four men testifying Friday to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s arrest and detention practices in Oregon said they were asked few, if any, questions before they were taken to detention facilities hours away from their homes.

Speaking through Spanish interpreters, the men — all in their 20s and 30s who work in blue-collar and service-connected jobs — said they still fear arrest by ICE and potential deportation, despite the fact that they are following immigration laws.

Their testimony bolstered arguments from a class of Oregon immigrants who want U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai to ensure the government is complying with his February injunction preventing ICE agents from arresting Oregon residents without a warrant and without determining whether they posed a flight risk.

The order provided them with new rules and parameters for how to perform an arrest that comported with the law.

A 34-year-old man from Venezuela, known only as JCCV, living in The Dalles, Oregon, with his family, said that he had a pending immigration application when he was inexplicably detained and taken to a Portland facility for multiple days.

He said agents mistook him for his brother, who is also living in the U.S., but didn’t bother to check his identification.

JCCV and other witnesses described being pressured by agents into signing a document for voluntary self-deportation.

“Before you signed it, did anyone explain to you that you were signing a document that would cause you to be removed from the country?” Kasubhai asked the man.

“No,” he said.

“What documents were the language in?”

“English.”

“Can you read English?”

“No.”

“Would you have signed the documents if they told you it was a form for voluntary departure?”

“No.”

Nelly Paola Garcia Orjuela, an attorney with the Innovation Law Lab, said the warrantless arrests were part of the Trump administration’s efforts to hit immigration arrest quotas to conform with the president’s sweeping deportation program.

“This meant a contingent of ICE agents were deployed to arrest many Oregonians without a warrant, detain them and transfer them out of state. Defendants did not discontinue this practice, and it’s because defendants continue to defy the law and are not complying with the law is why we are here today," Orjuela said.

Specifically, Orjuela accused ICE of making flight risk assessments of arrestees after their detention, applying improper flight risk standards, underreporting arrests and redacting and withholding arrest data meant to ensure compliance with the judge’s order, among other things.

Amber Qureshi, an attorney with the Deportation Data Project, which publicizes immigration enforcement data through Freedom of Information Act requests and other sources, testified there were 574 immigration arrests in Oregon between the judge’s February order and July.

Of those, 504 have been noncustodial arrests, which means they are more likely to have occurred without an arrest warrant, she explained.

At the end of an all-day evidentiary hearing, the judge signaled support for the request.

“At the minimum, the attention behind the document disclosure ordered in the preliminary injunction is not being met,” Kasubhai, a Joe Biden appointee, said. “I need to revisit what is being required to ensure the respondents are complying with my preliminary injunction.”

On cross-examination, the DOJ attorneys attempted to poke holes in witness testimony, questioning the validity and consistency of their statements.

“Plaintiffs bear the burden of demonstrating defendants have the violated injunction by clear and convincing evidence. They have not met that burden," DOJ attorney Ariana Garousi said.

Department of Justice attorneys argued that the men all had warrants for their arrest, which necessitated their detention.

Kasubhai also expressed confusion over ICE’s use of previously issued warrants to re-arrest immigrants.

“The idea that a warrant is issued and then someone is taken into custody and released generally means that the warrant is now resolved, and if somebody wanted to take that individual back into custody there would have to be an issuance of another warrant,” he said. “That doesn’t mean that the underlying issue has been resolved, but a new warrant has to be issued.”

But the DOJ attorneys argued that is not what Department of Homeland Security regulations require.

DOJ attorneys only called one witness, an ICE agent in the Medford, Oregon, known as JG who described the arrest of two of the witnesses. The hearing will continue Monday.

text:
President Trump has issued a proclamation that extends through September 21, 2027 a $100,000 fee for certain H-1B petitions, but due to an existing court order that vacated the fee policy under the prior proclamation, implementation of the $100,000 fee extension should also be barred. The new proclamation extends the September 2025 presidential proclamation that created the $100,000 H-1B fee and under which U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) collected the proclamation fee for nearly a year before being blocked by district court order in the summer of 2026.

USCIS remains barred from collecting the $100,000 H-1B fee under the September 2025 proclamation, which was due to expire on September 21, 2026. Since the new proclamation is issued as an extension, USCIS should be barred from collecting the $100,000 fee under the new proclamation as well. If USCIS takes the position that the new proclamation is outside of the purview of the existing court order, plaintiffs in the ongoing litigation are likely to quickly challenge that view.

During implementation of the September 2025 proclamation fee, the fee was requested and collected only by USCIS and only at the stage of petition adjudication. The fee was not requested by U.S. Customs and Border Protection or the Department of State and there is no indication of a mechanism for H-1B proclamation fee collection by these agencies. Should the immigration agencies take new positions or undertake new processes, these actions would be challenged in court by plaintiffs in the ongoing litigation challenging the proclamation fee.

On September 19, 2025, President Trump issued a proclamation that imposed a $100,000 fee on certain H-1B petitions from September 21, 2025 through September 21, 2026. The fee was generally imposed only on H-1B petitions that were filed for or only approvable for consular notification – petitions approved for changes of status or extensions of stay were exempt. Certain petitions were also determined to be exempt if filed on behalf of foreign nationals with valid H-1B visas.

In December 2025, a lawsuit was filed challenging the proclamation fee as an inappropriate exercise of power (State of California et al. v Markwayne Mullin, et al., Case No., 1:25-cv-13829 (D. Mass., filed Dec. 12, 2025)). On June 8, 2026, the federal district court vacated the H-1B proclamation fee policy in its entirety, taking the position that the $100,000 fee amounted to a tax, for which the proclamation and USCIS implementation were not a proper exercise of power, and that the policy violated the Administrative Procedure Act. Shortly thereafter, the district court stayed its own ruling, permitting USCIS to again collect the fee for a short time, but in July 2026, the Court of Appeals for the First Circuit refused to block the lower court ruling that vacated the $100,000 H-1B fee, again barring collection of the fee.

There should be no change to the status quo at this time; the new presidential proclamation extending the $100,000 H-1B proclamation fee policy should be subject to the existing court order blocking collection of the fee. However, as noted above, if the government takes a different position regarding the proclamation extension and policies, there could be confusion until clarity is sought and provided by the courts. In addition, USCIS continues to appeal the district court decision that vacated the $100,000 fee policy, so employers and foreign nationals should be aware that changes to the status quo are possible with little or no notice.

In addition, last month, USCIS separately proposed a regulation that would impose a fee of more than $103,000 on all cap-subject H-1B petitions. That fee would be separate from and in addition to the $100,000 H-1B proclamation fee, where applicable, if the proclamation fee were to be reinstated by further court order.

Fragomen is closely following all policy developments and litigation related to the H-1B program. Updates will be provided as developments occur.

A US federal appeals court has rejected the Trump administration’s policy of rapidly deporting migrants to countries other than their own – a ruling that could next go before the Supreme Court.

On Friday, a three-judge panel of the 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston largely upheld a February decision that found the Department of Homeland Security’s so-called third-country removal policy unlawful.

list 2 of 3US judge blocks Trump’s latest effort to limit birthright citizenship

list 3 of 3Trump administration proposes excluding certain immigrants from US census

The case stems from a class-action lawsuit testing what due process migrants are owed before being sent to nations with which they have no ties.

Writing for the panel, US Circuit Judge Seth Aframe said migrants must be given a “meaningful” chance to raise safety concerns before removal, rejecting the Trump administration’s narrower reading of the law.

The court did overturn part of the ruling on procedural grounds, concerning whether officials must first try deporting migrants to countries they have ties to.

Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said the decision confirmed that “due process and the protections Congress enacted against persecution and torture cannot be circumvented by putting someone on a plane to a country that was never part of their removal proceedings”.

The DHS did not immediately comment. The Trump administration is expected to appeal the ruling.

Under Trump, the US has struck agreements allowing it to send more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, most often Mexico, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a tracker run by the rights groups Refugees International and Human Rights First.

The policy, adopted in March 2025, allowed removals with only minimal notice if officials had diplomatic assurances against persecution.

The controversial programme has reached the Supreme Court twice.

In 2025, the justices cleared the way for eight men, including nationals of Cuba, Myanmar and Vietnam, to be deported to South Sudan, a country the US State Department advises against visiting because of “crime, kidnapping, and armed conflict”.

The DHS called the removals “a win”, while rights groups said they flouted basic protections.

The Trump administration’s immigration agenda has faced a string of setbacks this month.

A federal judge blocked planned caps on student and journalist visas, calling the government’s justification “exceptionally weak”, while a coalition of 22 states and Washington, DC, sued to stop a separate rule that would let officials deny green cards to immigrants who lawfully use public benefits.

text:
By Nate Raymond

BOSTON, Sept 18 (Reuters) – A US federal appeals court rejected on Friday a policy adopted by President Donald Trump’s administration that allows authorities to rapidly deport migrants to countries other than their own without giving them a chance to raise safety concerns.

Ruling in a case ​that is likely headed to the Supreme Court, a three-judge panel of the Boston-based 1st US ‌Circuit Court of Appeals largely upheld a February decision by a lower-court judge that declared the Department of Homeland Security’s policy unlawful.

The ruling came in a class-action lawsuit filed by migrants subject to deportation orders that has become a key test of what due process protections the government must provide before removing people to countries with which they have no connection.

“This decision confirms that ‌due process ​and the protections Congress enacted against persecution and torture cannot be circumvented ⁠by putting someone on a plane ⁠to a country that was never part of their removal proceedings,” Trina Realmuto, a lawyer for the plaintiffs at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, said

Under Trump, the administration has entered into a series of agreements that have allowed it to send more than 25,000 migrants to at least 29 third countries, ​in many cases Mexico, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal. Earlier in the same case, the administration twice convinced the ⁠Supreme Court to lift a preliminary injunction protecting migrants’ due process rights, clearing ⁠the way for eight men to be deported to South Sudan.

DHS had no ​immediate comment.

Under the third-country deportation program, DHS adopted a policy in March 2025 that would allow migrants to be sent to ​such countries if immigration authorities have credible diplomatic assurances they will not be persecuted ‌or tortured there.

The policy called for only minimal notice before a migrant could be sent to a third country that had not given the State Department such assurances.

THIRD COUNTRY DEPORTATIONS

US District Judge Brian Murphy, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, set aside the policy and concluded that it failed to protect migrants’ due process rights and could ⁠lead to their swift deportation to unfamiliar and potentially dangerous countries, without notice.

On appeal, the Trump administration contended that Murphy’s order if left intact would usurp its authority to execute potentially thousands of valid orders of deportation to ⁠third countries.

But US Circuit Judge Seth ‌Aframe, writing for Friday’s panel, said Murphy adopted a “sensible” interpretation of the immigration ⁠law requiring migrants be given a “meaningful” chance to raise any concerns before they ​are deported.

“DHS’s ‌proposed interpretation would deny access to that protection to a substantial swath of ​noncitizens who ⁠are sent to third countries with no notice of their destination,” Aframe wrote. “We decline to adopt such an interpretation.”

The panel included two Biden appointees, including Aframe, and a judge appointed by a Republican president.

However, the 1st Circuit overturned one part of Murphy’s ruling on procedural grounds. That part of the ruling concerned whether the government must first try to deport migrants to countries they have ties to before sending them to third countries.

(Reporting by Nate Raymond in ​Boston; Editing by Sanjeev Miglani)

text:
Read a PDF of our statement here.

Lawsuit argues that the federal government is intimidating voters and chilling civic participation, violating the Voting Rights Act

WASHINGTON, DC — Nine organizations representing immigrants, communities of color, and workers — the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), Mi Familia en Accion, OCA – Asian Pacific American Advocates, the National Urban League, Minnesota 8 (MN8), the Service Employees International Union, the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), the International Union of Painters (IUPAT), and the United Food and Commercial Workers International (UFCW)— filed a federal lawsuit today challenging the administration’s actions and statements that have put voters of color in reasonable fear that they will face federal interference when they go to vote, thereby chilling their participation in the upcoming midterm elections. The plaintiffs are represented by the Legal Defense Fund, Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund (AALDEF), Brennan Center for Justice at NYU Law, LatinoJustice PRLDEF, National Immigration Law Center (NILC), Protect Democracy, and Democracy Defenders Fund.

This lawsuit aims to protect and strengthen the freedom to vote, helping ensure that all communities can fully participate in our democracy with confidence.

The complaint documents how the federal government has asserted authority for armed agents to operate in the vicinity of voting locations, dismantled internal agency guardrails against election interference, and made unprecedented attempts to assert federal executive power over election administration. The result is predictable: voters across the country — especially Black, Latino, Asian American and Pacific Islander, immigrant, and naturalized citizen voters as well as voters from mixed-status families — fear questioning, arrest, detention, surveillance, or use of force by federal agents while casting their ballot on Election Day, conducting voter registration, or serving as an election official. Such harms violate Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act, which prohibits intimidation, threats, and coercion of people for voting or attempting to vote, as well as people who encourage or assist others in voting.

The lawsuit comes amid repeated assertions from federal officials across the administration about potentially deploying federal law enforcement in the vicinity of polling locations during the 2026 midterm elections. In the past year, the federal government has also repeatedly circumvented, or disregarded the law in carrying out arrests, investigations, and immigration enforcement actions.

Against that backdrop, the federal government’s statements threatening the presence of immigration agents and other law enforcement at polling locations undermine public confidence and deters eligible voters from participating in our democracy. The lawsuit calls on the courts to definitively prohibit the federal government’s threatened use of law enforcement at or around polling places.

View a copy of the full complaint here.

Co-Counsel Statements

“All American voters have the sacred right to have a voice in our democracy, and should be able to exercise that right freely and without fear,” said Janai Nelson, President and Director-Counsel of the Legal Defense Fund. “Using federal law enforcement as a scare tactic to target and intimidate Black communities is illegal and antithetical to the promise of a multiracial democracy that was enshrined in the Voting Rights Act. Neither Black, Latino, Asian, or any other voters nor any other communities should ever again face the threats of terror and intimidation at the ballot box that defined the Jim Crow era.”

“When the federal government puts fear between people and the ballot box, that is voter intimidation—plain and simple,” said Bethany Li, Executive Director of the Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund. “We are experiencing a level of voter intimidation like we haven’t seen since the civil rights era, when local governments and the KKK openly intimidated Black voters. This time, it is the federal government ordering ICE and other federal law enforcement to intimidate naturalized citizen voters and immigrant communities. In 2026, voters should not have to choose between their safety and their right to vote.”

“Election season political games are nothing new, but this administration has crossed a dangerous line undertaking a series of actions designed to target and terrify Latino voters,” said Lourdes M. Rosado, President and General Counsel, LatinoJustice PRLDEF. “Our community will not stand for lies about non-citizens voting in any substantial number, threats to deploy ICE at sensitive election locations, violent immigration enforcement tactics, and absence of safeguards against targeting naturalized and other American citizens. Congress prohibited voter intimidation in the Voting Rights Act at a time when the KKK terrorized Black voters, and it is shameful that today these protections are needed to stop our own federal government’s reign of terror.”

“Threatening, suggesting, or even hinting that ICE and other armed federal agents will be deployed to polling locations, contrary to federal law, is voter intimidation, plain and simple,” said Kica Matos, President of the National Immigration Law Center. “We will not be intimidated. When our right to vote is under attack, it is up to all of us to defend it. Let us make our voices heard at the ballot box and remind President Trump that voters pick our leaders and decide our future – not the other way around.”

“Instilling fear around voting is part of a broader strategy from the authoritarian playbook this Administration uses to disrupt our democracy,” said Hayden Johnson, Counsel at Protect Democracy. “We’ve seen communities join peacefully together to defend their rights over the last year and a half in the face of incursions from federal agents, and November will be no different.”

“Our laws prohibit intimidation or threats against any person exercising their right to vote. Deploying federal agents to polling places is unlawful and part of a broad scheme to deter eligible voters from making their voices heard,” said Amb. Norm Eisen (ret.), Executive Chair and Co-Founder of Democracy Defenders Fund. “This is a dangerous tactic in a long list of them by this administration intended to pre-determine the outcome of our elections.”

“The Trump administration has been waging a campaign to undermine American elections, and their insinuations that federal law enforcement agents might be at the polls this November are part of that effort,” said Jasleen Singh, Senior Counsel and Manager in the Brennan Center’s Democracy Program. “We’re bringing this lawsuit so that voters are protected against intimidation and can have their voices heard.”

Plaintiff Quotes

“We reject this administration’s attempt to desecrate our polling sites by converting them into militarized zones through the unlawful deployment of ICE or any other federal agent,” said Kristen Clarke, NAACP General Counsel. “The Voting Rights Act prohibits intimidation tactics that stand to deny and deter voters from exercising their voice and their rights. As a nation, we have no need for armed presence at polling locations — our elections are safe and transparent, which has been the hallmark of our democracy. Turning the fundamental right of exercising our vote into a high-stakes encounter with the militarized strong arm of the current administration isn’t protection and it isn’t oversight; it’s disenfranchisement, period. The NAACP calls on the court to reject this blatant attempt by federal officials to obstruct our elections through tactics pulled straight from the Jim Crow playbook.”

“Communities of color and immigrant communities have the right to vote, organize, and participate in our democracy without federal government intimidation,” said Thu Nguyen, Executive Director of OCA — Asian Pacific American Advocates. “The right to vote is the right to have a voice in the country we call home. Our communities should not have to fear that participating in our democracy could lead to baseless investigations, intimidation, or violence. We are asking the courts to give our communities the certainty they deserve that they will be able to safely exercise their right to vote on Election Day.”

“Voter intimidation is illegal, whether it comes from a mob outside the polling place or from the federal government itself,” said Marc H. Morial, President and CEO of the National Urban League. “Threatening to station ICE agents or other federal law enforcement near voting locations is a transparent attempt to sow fear, suppress participation, and silence communities whose voices are essential to a healthy democracy. Black Americans know the painful history of efforts to intimidate voters and deny equal access to the ballot. We will not allow those tactics to be repackaged for a new era. The National Urban League is proud to stand with our partners in defense of every American’s right to vote freely, safely, and without intimidation.”

“Latino voters have the same fundamental right as every American to cast their ballots freely and without intimidation. The presence of federal law enforcement at or near polling places risks creating fear and confusion, particularly in Latino and immigrant communities,” said Hector Sanchez Barba, President and CEO of Mi Familia en Acción. “Our message to Latino voters is clear: do not be intimidated. Know your rights, make a plan to vote, and make your voice heard. Mi Familia Vota will be on the ground in our communities working to protect access to the ballot and ensure every eligible Latino voter can exercise their right to vote safely and confidently.”

“Deploying federal agents to strike the fear of god into voters at polling places is a tactic straight out of the authoritarian playbook,” said AFT President Randi Weingarten. “It’s intimidation pure and simple and has no place in a true democracy. No matter your politics, American citizens need to be able to exercise their basic democratic right without running the gauntlet of an armed, masked militia. Our goal in this lawsuit is to ensure all those eligible to vote, particularly those covered by our Civil Rights laws, can access the ballot box free from coercion and interference. These midterms, we are doing everything we can to reassure Americans voting is safe and secure. And that when they turn out, hopefully in overwhelming numbers, the will of the people cannot be denied.”

“Minnesota 8 stands in steadfast solidarity with our national partners in this fight against voter intimidation,” said Dieu Do, Director of Programs at Minnesota 8. “As a Southeast Asian immigrant rights organization that bore witness to Operation Metro Surge, Minnesotans understand firsthand that this lawsuit represents our collective resistance to a federal government that is threatening our democracy’s future by attacking our constitutional right to vote, separating and deporting our immigrant families, and destabilizing our local communities. Our organizations will use every tool available to challenge this administration’s attempts to strip our humanity.”

“SEIU members are well aware of the threat of federal law enforcement at the ballot box later this fall. Our hard-working care and service workers, and the family and neighbors they’ll be voting alongside, won’t allow for intimidation when it comes to casting their votes,” said SEIU Executive Vice President Joseph Bryant. “No eligible voter should be afraid to make their voice heard. Voting is about accountability—about building a better future for our families. When that future and our rights are threatened, our members will throw down to stop such disenfranchisement. We hope that the court will protect our workers and communities around the country.”

“Over the last 18 months, the strategic deployment of federal agents has caused major disruptions for workers simply trying to provide for their families and support their communities,” said UFCW International President Milton Jones. “As we approach Election Day, these illegal intimidation tactics pose another hurdle for working people trying to make their voices heard at the ballot box. Everyone deserves to be able to cast their vote free from fear.”

“This is election interference pure and simple,” said IUPAT General President, Jimmy Williams, Jr. “We are a democratic union and have an obligation to stand up for democratic principles whenever they are attacked. Deploying federal agents to polling sites has no place in this country, it is authoritarian fearmongering and a blatant attempt to influence our elections. Our polling sites shouldn’t look like armed camps. American citizens have the right to engage in our democracy without having masked federal agents trying to deter them. Free and fair elections are a hallmark of our democracy and we cannot sit on the sidelines while this administration again attempts to game the system because they are worried about the results.”

text:
Outside the immigrant detention center in Tacoma on Wednesday, Humphrey Oyoo was trying to find his pregnant wife.

Cece Mokua, 29, had been detained the day before, while going to what was supposed to be an interview for her asylum application with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services — an agency that under past administrations was not involved with immigration enforcement and instead focused on adjudicating applications for legal status.

Instead, Mokua found herself dealing with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, who separated her from Oyoo and their 1-year-old, kept her for hours in a holding cell and took her to the Northwest ICE Processing Center.

But when Oyoo tried to leave a message for his wife Wednesday at the front desk of the Tacoma detention center, he was told she had been released. But had she really? Or was she being transferred to another ICE facility out of state? That has been happening to hundreds of people recently, and they too had usually been listed in the detention center’s system as “released.”

The front-desk officer couldn’t tell him.

About an hour later, Mokua called her husband. She truly was being released, but would remain in just-initiated deportation proceedings. He could pick her up in Tukwila.

So ended a confusing two-day ordeal for the couple, highlighting the unpredictability of current immigration enforcement tactics and the difficulty of getting information about people who have been detained. For a pregnant woman such as Mokua, the experience can be especially difficult. Mokua is five months pregnant and said she experienced contractions and a migraine while detained.

Supporters of the couple, including members of the activist group Defend Migrants Alliance who were at the detention center Wednesday with Oyoo, believe Mokua walked into a trap: a supposed asylum interview that was a pretext for her arrest.

“We have seen from time to time people called in for appointments with USCIS that really ended up being appointments for ICE to either arrest or initiate removal proceedings,” Matt Adams, legal director of the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project, said by email.

While not the norm, such ICE arrests across the country make it impossible to advise people on whether they might be detained in any particular situation, said Andrea Sáenz, a former member of the federal government’s Board of Immigration Appeals now working at Co-Counsel NYC, a New York-based legal services group.

The majority of people arrested by ICE locally and nationally in recent months have no criminal record. But someone who does, despite how old the charges or their level of severity, faces an increased risk of enforcement.

Mokua on New Year’s Day 2024 was charged with driving while under the influence, later amended to reckless driving, a gross misdemeanor. She said she was driving through fog on the wrong side of the road and crashed into the median when an oncoming car approached. She served no jail time, according to court records.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not provide answers this week to questions about Mokua’s arrest and detention.

A previous U.S. Department of Homeland Security statement commented generally on the detention of people with pending asylum applications, which was fairly unusual under past administrations. “To be clear, a pending application does NOT confer legal status in the United States. Any application for asylum does not preclude immigration enforcement,” the statement said.

ICE last month detained Kenyan physician and asylum applicant Robert Sidhe as he was returning to his Lynnwood home from the gym. In Seattle, he has worked as a patient care technician, assisting nurses, at UW Medicine. A federal judge ordered him released.

After Mokua’s arrest, SEIU 775 expressed concern about ICE enforcement against healthcare workers. Mokua does not work in healthcare, but her husband is a home healthcare aide and SEIU union member in Spokane, where the couple lives. He also runs an adult family home for seniors and others who can’t live on their own.

“We are already facing a shortage of caregivers as the population ages, and attacking immigrants will only deepen that shortage and make it harder for residents to get the care they need,” the union said in a statement.

According to Mokua, she came to the U.S. legally as a 15-year-old to live with an aunt in New Jersey and to escape female genital mutilation, a standard practice of her tribe. She finished high school in New Jersey and then college, majoring in biology, she said.

The aunt was supposed to make sure her young charge’s visa was renewed but would get irritated when Mokua asked about it. “So I stopped asking her,” Mokua said. Her visa expired.

From Kenya, her dad advised Mokua to apply for an internship anyway. Her employer would likely help her fix her status, her dad thought. But Mokua said she was distracted by college life and some difficult experiences that affected her mental health. She had a brief, unhappy marriage after college to a U.S. citizen who promised to help her achieve legal status but never did, Mokua said.

She moved to Spokane, where she has relatives, and several years ago met Oyoo on a dating app. They knew a lot of the same people. Oyoo, who said he is a green-card holder, is also from Kenya and lived for a time in New Jersey.

They had a baby, Josiah, and a month ago married. Meanwhile, Mokua said, she applied for asylum on the basis of her tribe’s female genital mutilation practices.

The family showed up to the scheduled USCIS interview with supporters who had invited the press to come. ICE had previously arrested at least a handful of Kenyans, they said, creating foreboding.

Oyoo and a recent law school grad accompanying them trailed behind Mokua as they went through the security line to get into the Department of Homeland Security’s regional headquarters in Tukwila. Mokua was focused on getting to the 7:30 a.m. appointment on time.

Oyoo had the baby and stroller, slowing him down. He handed the baby to the law school grad as he went through security and by the time he turned around, his wife was nowhere to be seen.

“Where did she go?” he thought.

He and the law school grad went to a second-floor waiting room. “By the time we were getting to the fifth hour, I knew there’s something wrong,” Oyoo recalled. He eventually got to an ICE officer to ask what was happening and was given a non-answer. He would have to wait for her call.

Mokua had been immediately approached by an officer, she said later. He led her up stairs to a waiting area and, in a few minutes, she was called into another room. This is her interview, she thought. But when the door opened, she saw two officers in ICE uniforms who told her she was under arrest.

She protested that she was there for an asylum interview and that her husband, child and lawyer were nearby. (The law school graduate was there for moral support, not to represent her.) But they pulled her arms behind her back, handcuffed her and took her through what she described as a back door. She did not tell them she was pregnant.

“I was scared and nervous,” she said.

She was taken to see an ICE officer, who began asking her when she had come to the U.S and why she fell out of status.

Then, Mokua said, she was placed in a cold, bare holding cell with concrete benches. She was offered noodle soup in a cup but turned it down. She had lost her appetite.

She stayed there until about 8 p.m., she said, as ICE arrested roughly 15 more people. They were men and were put in a separate holding cell. Eventually, ICE officers loaded them all onto a bus — chained and cuffed around their hands, waist and ankles — and took them to the detention center.

Mokua said the holding cell she went into there was even worse: “filthy, smaller.” Another long wait began while ICE processed what she said were some 30 people just arrested.

She said the only drinking water was from a sink above the toilet and she worried that was unsanitary. So she didn’t drink at all. The migraine and contractions started.

At that point, she made detention center officials aware of her condition and saw a detention center nurse. He didn’t give her any medicine, she said, but wrote a note saying she should have a bottom bunk when she got to her dormlike unit, making it easier to maneuver.

She reached the unit about 8 a.m., she said. The beds came with thin mattresses and no pillows, she said. The food served was cold and looked unappetizing. Again, she passed on eating. But there were books and games available as well as companionship with people from all over world.

She had a video call with her husband and Josiah. The 1-year-old cried.

By 12:45 p.m., she was told, without explanation, she was being released. She wondered if it was because officials realized she was pregnant.

The Trump administration has knowingly detained pregnant immigrants, disregarding a Biden-era policy. But the current administration has faced criticism for doing so and, after 18 miscarriages by detained pregnant women, has stopped tracking that figure, The Guardian reported this month.

Officers took Mokua back to the Homeland Security regional headquarters and then to a nearby building that houses a program ICE uses to monitor people in deportation proceedings who are not detained.

She came out with a watch monitor and a small bag of belongings, looking dazed. She wore a long, yellow sweater coat over her detention center uniform: a navy sweatshirt and sweatpants. Oyoo drove up with Josiah and she embraced her husband, then swooped Josiah into her arms.

Oyoo suggested they go to an Indian restaurant to get his wife’s favorite food. She hadn’t eaten in two days at this point.

The air was celebratory but Mokua’s mind was still on what lay ahead: a Monday check-in with ICE in Spokane. She didn’t think she could handle another surprise detention.

Federal

Investigation Finds ICE Detained Record Number of Pregnant Women While Losing Track of Miscarriage Data

According to an investigative report published on September 15, 2026, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has no current data on the number of miscarriages experienced by pregnant women in immigration detention; the most recent data are from October 2025. Present statistics show the rate of detained pregnant women is accelerating, causing some analysts to question the Department of Homeland Security’s adherence to a 2021 rule that limits the detention of pregnant individuals.

The causes of miscarriage are complex: it’s not possible to say that being in ICE detention causes miscarriage. Still, proper prenatal and emergency medical care can reduce the risk of miscarriage and other dangerous complications. According to first-hand accounts of detained women, such care was not provided even when they experienced experiencing severe pain and bleeding, typical symptoms of miscarriage. The findings come as ICE remains without permanent leadership: the White House withdrew its nomination of Lance Schroyer to head the agency on September 17, after his confirmation stalled in the Senate.

Legal

Court Halts DHS Rule Limiting Duration of Student Visa Stays

A federal judge in Massachusetts issued a nationwide preliminary injunction on September 14, blocking a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rule that would have capped F and J visas for international students and exchange visitors at four years and limited I visas for foreign journalists to 240 days, just one day before the rule was set to take effect. The judge ruled that a coalition of unions and higher education groups was “likely to succeed” on several grounds in their lawsuit challenging the rule, finding the government’s national security rationale “exceptionally weak” and calling the claim that the rule was necessary to safeguard national security something that “borders on the absurd”.

The ruling preserves the decades-old “duration of status” framework nationwide for now, meaning F-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors, and I-visa journalists continue to be admitted for the length of their academic program or qualifying employment rather than a fixed term. DHS and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) are barred from implementing or enforcing the rule while the litigation continues. The judge’s order postponed the rule’s effective date but denied, without prejudice, the plaintiffs’ request to permanently vacate the rule at this stage, meaning the injunction is a preliminary rather than final resolution of the case; the next court hearing is scheduled for October 2. The Trump administration is expected to appeal the decision.

Legal

DHS Watchdog Report Details Use of Small Cages at Alligator Alcatraz

A Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General report found that immigrants at the now-closed Florida detention center, Alligator Alcatraz, were being held in “small metal enclosures,” what facility staff called “calming areas” for anywhere between several minutes to nearly 2 hours. During an unannounced visit in January, the Inspector found that these enclosures were 4 feet 3 inches wide and 7 feet 9 inches tall. The report also found that Alligator Alcatraz did not comply with environmental health and safety standards as individuals in detention were not provided sufficient living space and spent most of their time in their units.

Oversight had largely been left to the state government. Governor Ron DeSantis’ Communications Director said they’d “make [the enclosures] smaller if they could.” The conditions at the facility raise alarms for the other state-run immigration detention centers such as Deportation Depot, a former prison in north Florida. The Inspector General wrote that although Alligator Alcatraz was closed in June of this year, the Deportation Depot has not been inspected.

ICE Surge in Indiana Sparks Calls for Transparency

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) announced this week that “Operation Safe Community-Indiana” resulted in 426 arrests statewide during a five-day sweep from August 30 to September 3, with most activity concentrated in the Indianapolis metropolitan area. ICE said those arrested had criminal histories and that some belonged to gangs including MS-13 and Tren de Aragua, though the agency did not specify what share of the 426 people had any criminal record at all. The operation was carried out in coordination with state and local law enforcement and came amid a broader summer surge in ICE enforcement nationally that has drawn less public attention than earlier mass deployments to cities like Minneapolis.

The scale and secrecy of the operation, which unfolded for days before ICE publicly acknowledged it, prompted sustained demands for transparency from Indianapolis officials, faith leaders, and members of Congress. More than 80 faith leaders in Indianapolis publicly criticized city officials for what they called a weak response, demanding guarantees that city resources were not being used to facilitate civil immigration enforcement, wider distribution of “Know Your Rights” materials, and a public hearing where residents could ask questions directly. Clergy also raised concerns about the Marion County Sheriff’s Office’s existing agreement to hold ICE detainees for up to 48 hours before many are transferred to the Miami Correctional Facility in Bunker Hill, and organizers held protests outside ICE’s Indianapolis office in the following weeks.

text:
A new Trump administration rule that is expected to make it harder for many legal immigrants to obtain green cards if they receive or are deemed likely to need public assistance went into effect Friday – even as lawsuits seeking to halt it wind their way through federal court.

The effort is one of President Donald Trump's latest moves to curb the number of immigrants in the US, including residents already living here legally.

What's more, the rule could prompt many green card applicants and their families to forgo receiving needed federal aid to avoid becoming considered "public charges" and hurting their chances of being approved.

unknown content item

-

Here's what you need to know about Trump's changes to the "public charge" rule:

What is a public charge?

Federal immigration officers have long reviewed green card applicants to ascertain whether they have the financial means to support themselves, among other considerations, to obtain permanent residency.

The Immigration Act of 1882 allowed the US government to deny entry to applicants deemed likely to be unable to take care of themselves and wind up dependent on government assistance – in other words, become "public charges."

In 1999, the Clinton administration defined a public charge as someone "primarily dependent" on government benefits. It considered only cash aid, such as Temporary Assistance for Needy Families or Supplemental Security Income, and Medicaid for long-term institutional care.

The first Trump administration sought to widen that definition to encompass non-cash benefits, such as food stamps, Medicaid and housing subsidies. It announced the broader rule in 2019 and put it into effect in 2020.

However, the following March, a federal court nullified the rule, and the Biden administration rescinded it. Biden officials then issued a new rule in 2022 limiting consideration to cash benefits only and clarifying that family members' use of federal benefit programs does not have an impact on applicants' reviews.

What does the new Trump administration rule do?

The new rule is similar to what was implemented by the first Trump administration but more expansive.

The latest rule, published in July, allows immigration officers to consider a wider array of public assistance programs when determining whether green card applicants will likely become "public charges." It also rescinds the 2022 rule.

"Under @POTUS Trump, DHS is restoring the basic principle that immigrants must be able to support themselves," the Department of Homeland Security posted to X at the time. "We are reaffirming the requirement of self-reliance, protecting public resources, and ending policies that encouraged dependency on hard-working American taxpayers."

The new rule does not specify which safety net programs should be considered, saying only that DHS "will consider the receipt of any means tested public benefits."

That could potentially include a wider array of income-based assistance, such as food stamps, Medicaid, childcare subsidies, housing vouchers and Head Start, as well as certain tax breaks, such as the child tax credit, Maddie Geschu, director of policy and advocacy at the Protecting Immigrant Families Coalition, told CNN in July.

Also, the new rule allows immigration officers to consider government benefits applied for on behalf of family members, including children who are citizens.

Who would be affected?

About 588,000 applicants are subject to public charge reviews annually, on average, according to DHS.

But the so-called "chilling effect" could have an even wider impact as applicants and their families opt to stay away from safety net programs for fear of being denied green cards.

DHS estimates that about 950,000 people may opt to leave or not enroll in six public benefits programs it examined, including Medicaid, food stamps, the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) and federal rental assistance.

Undocumented immigrants would not be affected since they do not qualify for public aid.

What are the concerns about the rule?

Immigration advocates fear that the rule will deter eligible family members from applying for or remaining enrolled in public safety net programs, including school meals and WIC, which provides nutrition assistance and counseling to pregnant women, new mothers and young children.

"No parent should ever have to choose between feeding their children and keeping their family together," Clarissa Hayes, deputy director of child nutrition programs and policy at the Food Research & Action Center, told reporters earlier this week. "We cannot allow fear and confusion to determine whether or not a child will have enough to eat."

Also, the revised rule "really opens the green card process to abuse based on partisan politics or personal bias," Geschu told reporters.

Earlier research on the prior Trump administration rule found that participation in programs among immigrant families and citizen children declined in 2019 and 2020, even among those not subject to it at the time, the advocates said.

Similarly, the latest effort would have widespread consequences. Some 3.7 million members of immigrant households could lose Medicaid, food stamps, housing benefits and other assistance, according to a George Washington University study published in December that analyzed the proposed rule. State economies could lose $27.4 billion as healthcare providers, grocery stores and other businesses lose revenue. Up to 212,000 jobs could be lost.

Why have some states and cities filed lawsuits?

A coalition of 22 states and the District of Columbia, led by New York, are suing to block the rule. A group of cities, led by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, has filed a similar lawsuit. They were both filed Monday in the Southern District of New York.

The states argue they would lose billions of dollars in federal funding if immigrants, particularly mixed-status families, disenroll from safety net programs due to fears about immigration consequences. And they say that the new rule gives "unfettered discretion for immigration officials to determine who can be excluded on public charge grounds."

The determinations could "fundamentally depart from the core meaning of the term" public charge, according to the filing.

The cities, meanwhile, say in their filing that the rule will harm their public health and economic interests, including shifting costs for healthcare, food and housing to the cities and hurting their labor forces.

A group of advocacy organizations filed their own lawsuit against the rule in the Southern District of New York on Thursday, arguing it violates the Immigration and Nationality Act.

"At its core, this new rule is cruel: at a time when the cost of everything— from food to housing to healthcare — is unbearably high, immigrant families and U.S. citizen children will be punished for accessing these basic necessities," Rebecca Telzak, co-executive director of Make the Road New York, said in a statement.

What happens next?

The rule went into effect on Friday.

Federal District Court Judge Ronnie Abrams of the Southern District of New York, an Obama appointee, set an initial conference for October 9 for the lawsuit brought by the states.

CNN's Gloria Pazmino contributed to this report.
